articles.title_orig: What China’s Vibe-Coding Capital Can Tell Us About the A.I. Boom
articles.title_zh: What China’s Vibe-Coding Capital Can Tell Us About the A.I. Boom
articles.content_orig:
In mid-May, days after Donald Trump visited Beijing, a Chinese tech founder named Levy invited me to an office party for his A.I. fortune-telling company. It’s called FateTell, and it makes an app that, in the vein of traditional Chinese astrology, reads your bazi, a chart that tracks the elemental forces associated with your birth date and time. (Levy wanted me at the event because of the makeup of my bazi. According to his invitation, my governing element, fire, would counteract the water element that Levy carries in oversupply.) So I travelled from Beijing to FateTell’s headquarters, situated on the edge of Hangzhou—one of China’s tech hubs, home to Alibaba and the insurgent Chinese A.I. company DeepSeek—in a town called Liangzhu.
Liangzhu means “beautiful waterland,” and it more than earns the name—rivers, lakes, and marshes thread through the low hills at the town’s edge. The town is hip, idyllic, contrarian, and increasingly known as an escape for workers burnt out by the grind of China’s booming tech industry. To those back in Beijing or Shenzhen, Liangzhu has become a low-cost retreat where people can afford to vibe-code—building software through conversations with A.I., as opposed to writing source code at a line-by-line level–on their own terms, without having to work what is known as the 9-9-6, an extreme schedule that is common in Chinese tech firms of working from 9 A.M. to 9 P.M., six days a week.
Residents often dub themselves “villagers,” and describe Liangzhu as between rural and suburban. Between verdant parks and wide avenues, they sit on sprawling grass fields—a way of relaxing that is rare in most major Chinese cities, where lawns are usually cordoned off. Often, there is a stroller parked next to them. (China’s birth rate has plummeted to its lowest point since 1949, but, in the area where Liangzhu is, the birth rate is double the national average).
It didn’t take me long after my arrival in Liangzhu to stumble upon the town’s growing population of vibe-coders. Near Liangzhu’s cultural and art center, a sprawling structure designed by Tadao Ando and surrounded by cherry blossoms, I overheard young developers murmuring about Kimi, a Chinese large language model, and OpenAI’s Codex. Some had dogs at their feet. Others were coding over oat-milk lattes. The building’s nickname, I learned, is the Big Roof. Nearby stands another towering structure, called the Big Barn, which contains a vast bookstore. The structures, made of raw concrete, exuded an ostentatious form of modesty, emblematic of the town’s character.
Everywhere I went, people were building new A.I. products. This is not unique to Liangzhu. In the past few years, as the A.I. boom went global, Beijing has made A.I. a national priority, launching a campaign known as A.I. Plus to seed it throughout the economy. China’s major tech companies are bracing for the same transformation, pouring money into semiconductors, large language models, and cloud infrastructure, as well as the consumer products that are built on top of them. But, unlike the everything apps that are favored by most of these big tech companies, much of the software built in Liangzhu is whimsical and quirky, similar in spirit to an artisanal craft you might pick up at a small-scale farmers’ market. FocusFlight, a timer that simulates an immersive flight environment to improve concentration, plays white noise while you “fly” to a city. (As I wrote this piece, I “flew” from San Francisco to Los Angeles.) YouMind, an A.I. workflow tool, bills itself as a “second brain” that helps people “create bolder” by gathering scattered reading, notes, and research in one place and turning it into finished work (one of their ads is an A.I.-generated video that tells the story of an exhausted mother with no income, trying to write as a baby cries in the background; later, she is pictured using YouMind, and becomes happy and successful). And then there is FateTell, which feeds your bazi through large language models and spits out guides “based on thousands of years of Eastern wisdom.” The app has hundreds of thousands of users, the most devoted of whom pay an annual fee to subscribe. (Levy told me they’re also exploring a hardware direction: making wooden blocks shaped like moons—traditional divination tools that are thrown to seek spiritual guidance—embedded with smart chips.)
In fact, a throwback to traditional Chinese spirituality and Western New Age practices pervades much of the town. I checked a local event guide during my visit; it included an I Ching guide to dressing for luck, a Zen sutra reading, and an essential-oils workshop for healing. A singing-bowl sound-therapy studio sat beside a boutique that sold only linen and silk clothing, cut loose and draping enough to make the wearer look faintly monk-like. Crystals were in one shop window; tarot upstairs. Astrology, consumerism, and A.I. were folded into one another as though they had always belonged together—reminiscent of an older era of Silicon Valley when spirituality and personal computing grew out of the same countercultural milieu. I asked Ian Johnson, a Canadian-American reporter who won a Pulitzer Prize for his coverage of Chinese religious life in the early two-thousands, about the way spirituality was manifesting among young people in the A.I. generation. “They’re like the Woodstock generation in the West,” he told me. Johnson explained that the previous generation in China underwent rapid economic development and huge leaps in the availability of material goods. For their children, existential questions have emerged, and in the fast-moving, chaotic tech world, he added, uncertainty feels especially acute. “Why one company succeeds and another fails can seem almost metaphysical,” Johnson said.
Levy, the founder of FateTell, is a star in Liangzhu. A graduate of the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology, he once worked at ByteDance, the company that created TikTok. He is lean, with a slight frame and a calculating gaze—though he speaks softly and contemplatively. He told me he has long been interested in how technology intersects with spirituality, referencing both the I Ching and Frank Herbert’s “Dune,” and, after I told him that I live in the Bay Area, he said, with a small conspiratorial grin, that he had cast the bazi of every major A.I. leader. His reading of Sam Altman’s bazi: “a mercenary accountant.” Elon Musk, he said, “will have a very bumpy few years.” He had almost named the company Muad’Dib, after the nickname that the character Paul Atreides takes among the Fremen in “Dune,” but FateTell had the benefit of being slightly more literal.
At the party, Levy introduced me to the FateTell team, a group of eight people, among whom almost no moment goes un-astrologized. One engineer took a two-week vow of silence because his bazi had warned him that he was losing his sense of self by excessively describing his life—an increasingly common affliction for a generation immersed in Chinese social media. All eight employees had had their charts checked for compatibility before being hired. The C.O.O. treated my bazi as if it were as important as my last name and warned me, “The Year of the Fire Horse might bring you fame, but also exhaustion and illness.”
Before entering the tech world, Levy had considered becoming a Taoist monk. “Years ago, a great master told me I had a gift for the spirit,” he said. “He nearly took me up into the mountains to cultivate the Tao.” But Levy’s love of A.I. proved the stronger pull, and he instead attempted to merge Taoism with that. “I’ve wanted to build a Taoist app since 2017,” he explained. “The years since have been preparation—I met hundreds of practitioners and diviners, and read my way through the classical scriptures.” Then, after DeepSeek launched, he was convinced that the time had finally come.
It was late 2024, a year after Xi Jinping had named A.I. an essential engine for China’s “new quality productive

articles.title_orig: Mamdani roasted for staying tight-lipped on 'war criminal' Pezeshkian after raging about Netanyahu
articles.title_zh: Mamdani roasted for staying tight-lipped on 'war criminal' Pezeshkian after raging about Netanyahu
articles.content_orig:
Fox News correspondent Alexis McAdams reports on New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani calling for the arrest of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ahead of his visit to the United Nations. Israeli Ambassador to the U.N. Danny Danon joins 'America Reports' to react to the controversial comments and discuss the threat of Iran-backed attacks against regional allies.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani repeatedly branded Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a "war criminal," but faced criticism for remaining largely tight-lipped about Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian’s visit to New York for the United Nations General Assembly.
While Mamdani has labeled the Iranian government "brutal" and cited its "systematic repression of its own people," critics railed against him for declining to use similar language about Pezeshkian, who arrived in the city on Wednesday.
"Mayor Mamdani, you said war criminals who set foot in New York should be arrested. Good news. One is in New York city this week," said Iranian-born journalist Masih Alinejad, who was subjected to an assassination attempt near her Brooklyn home while Ayatollah Ali Hosseini Khamenei was still alive.
"If you have the courage to talk about arresting those responsible for crimes against humanity, start with the man sleeping five miles from your office," Alinejad tweeted .
TRUMP, IRANIAN PRESIDENT CONVERGE ON NYC FOR ‘DRAMATIC’ UN SHOWDOWN AS TEHRAN FACES TIGHT RESTRICTIONS
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani branded Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu a "war criminal" and urged the federal government to arrest him under an International Criminal Court warrant on July 21, 2026. ((L) Reuters, (R) @NYCMayor via X)
She invited Mamdani to view the FBI files about her case, in which several men attempted to kidnap her in Brooklyn.
Director of National Intelligence Walter "Jay" Clayton said in January that the Iranian regime coordinated a murder-for-hire plot against Alinejad because of her efforts to speak out against its human rights abuses, while federal authorities sentenced one U.S.-based conspirator to 15 years.
"The government of Iran, a sponsor of terrorism, assassination, and espionage around the globe, has engaged in a campaign of assassination plots in the United States and abroad targeting those who oppose the regime," Clayton said in a statement.
MAMDANI MAKES EYEBROW-RAISING CLAIM ABOUT NETANYAHU PROTESTS AHEAD OF NYC VISIT
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian speaks during celebrations marking the 46th anniversary of the 1979 Islamic revolution in Tehran, Iran, on Feb. 10, 2025. (Iranian Presidency/Anadolu via Getty Images)
Meanwhile, Mamdani has said Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City and has called him an "architect" of "genocide." No similar statements about Pezeshkian could be found.
Fox News Digital reached out to Mamdani for comment.
National security expert and ACT For America founder Brigitte Gabriel also criticized the mayor over the discrepancy.
Gabriel, who has said she survived a terror attack during the 1975 Lebanese Civil War in Lebanon, now lives in the U.S.
"[The] Iranian President on American soil — while we are still in open conflict with Iran. 18 Americans dead. Thousands of Iranians slaughtered. And he’s getting a visa, a hotel, and a UN microphone in New York," Gabriel fumed on X.
"Where are the war crimes charges? Where’s Mamdani to arrest him while he’s in NYC?"
ISRAEL'S AMBASSADOR SAYS NYC’S MAMDANI IS ‘SOWING CHAOS’ AHEAD OF NETANYAHU’S UN APPEARANCE
Masih Alinejad, a prominent Iranian American human rights activist, attends an interview with the Associated Press in Berlin, Germany, on Nov. 9, 2024. (AP Photo/Ebrahim Noroozi, File)
Israeli U.N. Ambassador Danny Danon told reporters Tuesday that Mamdani should stop attacking his nation’s government and turn his attention to Pezeshkian’s administration.
"Focus on the problems of the City of New York and stop with promoting anti-Semitism, stop supporting Hamas , and stop engaging with the Iranian regime," Danon said.
Those comments came weeks after Mamdani’s international affairs liaison sought to arrange a meeting with Iranian U.N. Ambassador Amir-Saeid Iravani .
Senate Intelligence Committee Chairman Tom Cotton told Fox News the disparity in Mamdani’s rhetoric is stark.
TRUMP TO MEET WITH MAMDANI IN NEW YORK AMID HIGH-STAKES MIDTERM PUSH
"Is Zohran Mamdani threatening to arrest butchers from Iran who have killed tens of thousands of their own people, or genuine war criminals from other countries?" Cotton, R-Ark., asked.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
President Donald Trump and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani meet at Gracie Mansion on Sept. 21, 2026.
"No. The one person he cites is the leader of the Jewish State of Israel."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While Mamdani met with President Donald Trump on Tuesday, he said afterward the two leaders will continue to have radically different views on Israel and the conflict in Iran.
Born and raised in Allentown, Pennsylvania, worked in both the New York and Washington bureaus for Fox News since 2013.

articles.title_orig: Tim Janus, competitive eating champion and ‘The Amazing Race’ competitor, dead at 49
articles.title_zh: Tim Janus, competitive eating champion and ‘The Amazing Race’ competitor, dead at 49
articles.content_orig:
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Tim Janus, the world champion competitive eater known as “Eater X” who competed alongside Joey Chestnut, has died at age 49.
Janus, who lived in the East Village in NYC, died on Sept. 16 following a long battle with cancer, per Major League Eating .
He peaked at the No. 2 ranking in the world as a competitive eater, behind only Chestnut, who he teamed with on “The Amazing Race 30” in 2017, coming in fifth place.
Janus held titles in tiramisu eating, ramen eating, nigiri sushi eating and burping.
He was also a regular at the Nathan’s Hot Dog Eating Contest, where he finished second to Chestnut in 2010 and third to him in 2014.
Janus was committed to eating anything.
“I’d eat a roll of pennies if I thought I could set a world record, taste doesn’t matter,” he told Food Republic in 2015. “I’d like to eat everything in the world at least once. I’d eat alien if we could find it. If we could raise dinosaurs, I’d sign up to eat those.”
Janus’ career lasted from 2006-18 and he was later inducted into the Major League Eating Hall of Fame.
His signature look on stage was a painted Viking mask face, inspired by his love of wrestling as a child.
“I tell people that I learned a lot about life by eating hot dogs, and I mean it,” he said at his induction. “If you care about something and work hard at it, it makes you better.”
According to the Daily Mail, Janus tweeted in 2016 that he feared the impact competitive eating would have on his body.
“Deep down I’ve wondered how long-term stupid competing is for my health. I can’t ignore that feeling anymore,” he wrote. “For me it’s more about how we’re destroying our bodies. Each of us only gets one,”
Janus retired from the sport two years later and was accepted by the United States Foreign Service, though those plans were halted when he was diagnosed with cancer.
“Tim followed his own passions and dreams without regard for the pressures or expectations of society,” recalled Crazy Legs Conti, Janus’s ex-roommate and former world oyster-eating champion.
“He was unique, brilliant, and beloved by his friends. He lived his life on his own terms.”

articles.title_orig: ‘Dammit, something has to happen’: White House preparing plan for 90-day diesel exports ban
articles.title_zh: ‘Dammit, something has to happen’: White House preparing plan for 90-day diesel exports ban
articles.content_orig:
The oil industry has warned a diesel export ban will backfire and exacerbate the global fuel crisis as President Donald Trump weighs restrictions.
Trump appeared to back an export ban earlier this week, as he faces mounting political pressure to tackle rising fuel prices ahead of the midterm elections in November.
"I've said let's not send out the diesel. We make a lot of diesel," Trump told reporters Tuesday on the sidelines of the annual United Nations General Assembly. "I've called for it within my people. I've been talking about it."
The American Petroleum Institute, an oil lobby group, quickly pushed back after Trump's comments. API CEO Mike Sommers warned "restricting U.S. energy exports would only compound the problem—exacerbating refining challenges and ultimately hurting consumers."
"The answer is more supply and more flexibility—not new restrictions that risk making a difficult situation worse," Sommers said in a statement Tuesday.
The stocks of U.S. refiners Valero, Marathon Petroleum and Phillips 66 fell Wednesday after Politico reported that the Trump administration is preparing a plan to ban diesel exports for 90 days.
But Energy Secretary Chris Wright told The Wall Street Journal that the Trump administration was considering restrictions rather than an outright export ban.
"We're trying to avoid a blunt hammer of a government policy, understanding the complexity of refining," Wright told the Journal on Wednesday.
An export ban would result in "more expensive gasoline right away," the Energy secretary said last week. U.S. refineries would cut production, including gasoline, as storage tanks are filled, said Wright, an industry insider who previously served as CEO of the oilfield services firm Liberty Energy.
"If you start putting barriers on flows, pretty quickly you will reduce the production, and you'll have less supply," Wright told The Daily Caller in an interview on Sept. 17.
An oil industry executive told CNBC's Brian Sullivan that a diesel export ban could raise the price of fuel by 30 cents per gallon. Gasoline prices could rise toward record levels if an export ban is implemented, said Patrick De Haan, head of petroleum analysis at GasBuddy, in a social media post.
An export ban would briefly lead to a price collapse but likely only on the Gulf Coast where there's a lot of refining capacity and the lower Midwest, said Bob McNally, president of Rapidan Energy and former energy advisor to President George W. Bush. The Northeast will likely not see much relief because the region is more dependent on imports, the analyst said.
After some brief relief in certain regions of the U.S., prices will rise to levels higher than they would have been otherwise as refiners cut production, McNally said. Prices will "soar globally," he said.
And there's a risk that U.S. trade partners could retaliate, McNally said. The U.S. exports diesel to Europe and the Europeans export gasoline to the U.S.
There is concern in the oil industry that Europe could ban gasoline exports to the U.S., the analyst said. This would be particularly problematic for the more import-dependent U.S. Northeast, he said.
But the White House faces mounting pressure from a growing group of Republican lawmakers to implement an export ban as diesel prices have reached record highs ahead of the midterm elections.
This past weekend, Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa for the White House to "embargo diesel" to help farmers. Iowa is one of the biggest farming states in the U.S., diesel is crucial for agriculture, and Republicans face a very competitive senate race in the Hawkeye State despite voters there backing Trump three times.
Diesel cost $6.52 per gallon on average nationwide Wednesday, nearly $3 more expensive than this time last year, according to data from AAA. Gas cost $4.47 per gallon, $1.30 more expensive than the same period in 2025.
"It's panic," McNally said. "It's a tough election and historically rising diesel prices. It's full-blown panic."
It's still not clear what course of action Trump will ultimately take.
The White House is examining whether an export ban is "feasible in terms of the overall refining capacity and whether a full or partial ban would work," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Tuesday when asked by Trump to explain the administration's deliberations to the press.
A White House official told CNBC on Wednesday that Trump "wants to see gas prices at the pump fall and is evaluating all the options on the table."
One of the key reasons why diesel prices are so high right now is because Russia banned exports due to Ukraine's attacks on its refineries.
Moscow's ban removed the second-largest source of diesel from the global market. A U.S. export ban would compound the problem by removing the biggest source of diesel from the market.
"I don't know of an oil economist or expert or analyst who actually understands oil who thinks it's a good idea," McNally said. "I think there's widespread opposition, even in the administration."

articles.title_orig: CNN, Politico and MS NOW to face off with Trump administration in court over White House ban
articles.title_zh: CNN, Politico and MS NOW to face off with Trump administration in court over White House ban
articles.content_orig:
The trio of media outlets that President Donald Trump abruptly banned from accessing the White House will be in court Wednesday to argue their expulsion was unconstitutional and should be lifted immediately.
“This ban could not be a more direct assault on the First Amendment nor a more blatant violation of our most fundamental constitutional principles,” lawyers for CNN, Politico and MS NOW said in a court filing Monday ahead of the hearing.
“The ban is unconstitutional and should be immediately restrained,” they contended, citing legal precedent in the District of Columbia and U.S. Supreme Court.
The news organizations are scheduled to make their case to U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly at a 3:30 p.m. ET hearing.
Late Tuesday, the Justice Department defended the ban in a court filing, arguing that Trump had decided the outlets “failed to maintain basic minimum ‘standards of professionalism and decorum expected of those given access to the White House Complex, including’ by ‘publishing sensitive or classified information.’”
The outlets’ “access to the White House is a privilege — not a right,” the filing said.
On Tuesday, the White House Press Office sent letters to the three outlets alleging their coverage involved “trafficking in verifiable falsehoods about national security and other issues, and publishing sensitive or classified information,” the department said in the filing. The letters also were filed in court.
The articles cited in the letters included reporting on the construction of the White House ballroom and its related military security complex, the status of munitions supplies being used in the Iran war, an alleged FBI leak investigation involving a journalist, and sanctions on Russia.
In the letters, the administration gave the organizations a deadline of 5 p.m. Friday to “contest this initial decision” to bar them from the White House or the decision “will be final,” the filing said.
The outlets did not immediately respond to NBC News’ requests for comment on the allegations in the filing.
Ahead of the court hearing, more than four dozen media outlets and groups filed a friend of the court brief urging the judge to side with the banned outlets. NBCUniversal Media, the parent company of NBC News, was among the groups that took part in the brief.
The administration’s reason for the ban, the filing said, was “transparently viewpoint discriminatory.”
“The current ban — and any future bans — are intended to impair the critical work of news organizations covering the presidency if this Court does not immediately intervene,” the group wrote in the filing.
Kelly was nominated to the bench by Trump in his first term but ruled against him in a similar case back in 2018, when the White House pulled press credentials from then-CNN reporter Jim Acosta.
In a post on Truth Social on Monday, Trump said Kelly is a “great judge” for the media outlets, and suggested he believes he’ll rule against his administration. “[A]s usual, we’ll go for appeal,” he wrote, “because Fake News people and publications that only write negatively” should not be “allowed access to the most important Office anywhere in the World.”
Trump also criticized the judge as “totally disloyal” in a separate post late Tuesday.
The three news organizations have pointed to similar remarks by Trump as proof they’re victims of impermissible “viewpoint discrimination.”
Trump announced the outlets’ ban from the White House in a Truth Social post Friday, and said it was “a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”
“Other Fake News Media Outlets to follow,” he added.
Responding to questions from a reporter in the Oval Office a short time later, Trump referred to it as “the ban on the free press.” “Very simple ban. I don’t want them in my office. I don’t want them here,” he said.
He said the policy was in response to “cumulative stories over the last few years.”
“They purposely write negative news. And they do that because they want to try and diminish the Republicans and a Republican administration,” he said. “If they could straighten themselves out, I’d love it,” he added.
The outlets’ suit said Trump’s “words leave no doubt that banning Plaintiffs from the White House is retaliation for their protected newsgathering and speech — retaliation that is intended to cow them into changing their reporting and threaten other journalists lest they suffer the same fate. That is a paradigmatic First Amendment violation” and “flatly unconstitutional.”
The ban has already impacted news coverage, the suit says.
CNN is a member of the five-network rotation “for the primary television pool (also called the network pool) and absorbs 20% of the costs associated with such coverage,” the suit says.
The pool covers “events and locations where there is limited physical space for journalists,” their court papers say, and for “most of what the President does each day, the pool is the only source of independent reporting, video, and photographs available to the press and the public.”
“When CNN is the designated network pooler, CNN’s crew supplies the video and audio of the events involving the President and other White House officials to the other four networks and, through them and through pool distribution arrangements, to news organizations and the public. Among the recipients of the pool material are the more than 1,000 local affiliate television stations across the United States that receive the pool feed through CNN.”
NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox News are the other members of the rotation.
MS NOW is a rotating member of the secondary pool, while Politico is a member of the rotating print pool.
CNN had been scheduled to be the pool camera Monday, and the other networks in the TV network pool jointly declined to step in and replace its coverage, resulting in Trump’s remarks at a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the White House being inaudible.
His remarks at the United Nations on Tuesday and alongside New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani at a press conference Monday were picked up by U.N. cameras and local news outlets, respectively.
Trump defended the bans in a social media statement Monday and added a new argument — that “fake news” is a national security issue.
“The White House is not instituting an assault on the Free Press, something which I cherish. It is instituting an assault on the FAKE NEWS, something that has grown like Cancer in our beloved United States of America,” he wrote. “It is a threat to our National Security, and must be stopped, NOW!”

articles.title_orig: Trump lawyers defend president banning journalists from White House ahead of court hearing – live
articles.title_zh: Trump lawyers defend president banning journalists from White House ahead of court hearing – live
articles.content_orig:
Trump lawyers defend president banning journalists from White House ahead of court hearing – live
Trump lawyers say White House access is ‘a privilege, not a right’; CNN, Politico and MS Now to present case in court after president banned outlets from White House grounds
Trump administration calls banned journalists' White House access 'a privilege, not a right,' brands coverage a security risk
In a new legal filing in the case over a trio of new outlets barred entry to the White House, Trump administration lawyers repeatedly defended the president’s ban by saying journalists were not entitled to access to the building.
“Access to the White House is a privilege, not a right,” the filing stated.
The filing went on to assert that the three outlets – by publishing sensitive or classified information obtained through its reporting – constituted a national security threat, giving the president the right to ax their credentials.
Trump banned the three outlets – CNN, MS Now, and Politico – last Friday in a snap decision announced via social media. He branded the three outlets “fake news” and threatened future bans against other outlets could follow.
Early the following week, the three publications filed a joint lawsuit asking a federal judge to restore their access, alleging that the action was an illegal act of retaliation that violated their First Amendment rights. A president, they argued in their complaint, can’t bar access to journalists based on reporting he doesn’t like.
Since then, Trump has found himself in an escalating tit-for-tat with the press, which has responded to the ban with measures of solidarity. Several outlets have declined to publish any images or video of the president so long as the three outlets are denied access to the White House. And the members of Trump’s standard TV pool – five channels, including CNN, who take turns traveling with the president, filming his daily activities, and distributing that footage – have ceased their duties.
Trump administration drafting up plans for 90-day embargo on diesel exports: report
The Trump administration is readying to launch a 90-day ban on diesel fuel exports from the United States, following mounting calls from his party to take action to bring down the fuel’s price ahead of the midterm elections, POLITICO reported Wednesday.
Several people with inside knowledge of the conversations told POLITICO (currently one of three outlets banned from the White House by Trump) that the plan has created a schism within pro- and anti-embargo camps in the administration. It’s also prompted furor from the oil and gas industry that has broadly supported the president.
One oil industry executive privy to the conversations told the outlet that Trump seemed intent on announcing a ban by the end of the week.
The price of fuel has weighed heavily on Republicans in the lead-up to the midterms, which will determine whether Trump’s party retains control of Congress for the second half of his term. Trump ran in 2024 in part on bringing down the price of gas, but the war he helped kick off between the US and Iran, and the closure of vital oil shipping arteries it prompted, has sent the cost of fuel skyrocketing.
Diesel, in particular, has become a sore spot. The fuel for everything from semi-trucks to tractors to heavy machinery, it has surged in price even more than standard gasoline, to more than $6.50 per gallon.
That’s prompted some Republicans, especially those representing farming-heavy states, to publicly call on the president to take drastic action to lower the price of diesel.
The pushback, POLITICO reports, is coming from oil and gas executives and administration officials who warn that the embargo could raise fuel prices in the long run.
Yesterday, Britain’s new prime minister Andy Burnham navigated his way through a first high-stakes meeting with DonaldTrump at the UN general assembly in New York. His aides were delighted with how the meeting went, as Trump praised the US-UK relationship and described Burnham as a “natural businessman”.
The anticipated sticking points – theChagos Islands, WestBank settlement sanctions and Ireland – appear not to have derailed the talks nor cast a shadow over the future relationship.
In today’s edition of The Latest podcast, Lucy Hough speaks to the our policy editor in London, Kiran Stacey. You can also watch on YouTube.
'I am the code': Trump reportedly clashed with White House ballroom architect after dismissing safety concerns
The Washington Post (paywall) reports today that James McCrery II, the first architect on Donald Trump’s controversial $400m White House ballroom project, resigned after repeatedly clashing with the president, who dismissed his warnings that design features Trump was insisting on violated building safety codes.
McCrery withdrew from the project last October after warning Trump that a preliminary design he wanted “did not provide adequate emergency exit routes or fire-containment measures”, according to the Post’s report, which cites two people with knowledge of the discussions and corroborating documents reviewed by the paper.
The sources said Trump brushed off the architect’s concerns, and argued that no building codes apply to White House construction. “I am the code,” Trump reportedly said.
The Post previously reported that they had also clashed over the size of the ballroom. One document obtained by the paper features an image of a planned data center overlaid on a map of Manhattan, with a note that appears to be poking fun at McCrery’s concerns. “James,” it reads. “And you think we are big.”
Another note made in Sharpie makes clear Trump’s preference for Corinthian-style columns.
When approached by the Post, McCrery didn’t say why he stepped down. A White House official said it was “factually false and totally inaccurate” to suggest he left the project over issues with the code, and said he was a “valued member of the initial design team.”
Discussions about the safety issues continued for months after McCrery’s departure, according to White House records reviewed by the Post.
It is not clear from those records whether the safety issues he identified have been resolved in more recent designs by Shalom Baranes Associates, the architecture firm that took over McCrery’s firm’s role in the project late last year.
The ballroom project is – unusually – being overseen by the Executive Residence, rather than the General Services Administration or National Park Service. The small office is exempt from rules that require federal agencies to solicit competitive bids and disclose details to the public, the Post previously reported. Typically, it’s responsible for routine repairs, entertainment expenses, and the purchase of furniture, art and other items for the executive mansion.
Rubio, in his press conference, also touched on the war in Iran at several points, including on the surprise negotiations that took place yesterday between Trump administration envoys and the Iran delegation.
“I don’t want to mischaracterize this as a major breakthrough,” Rubio said. “But at the same time I think it was significant that at least there was a conversation.”
Little detail has been shared about what was discussed at that meetings, though Rubio framed the conversation as a continuation of the earlier back-and-forth between the two sides.
Rubio also notably insisted that Trump would be able to see through his campaign in Iran acting on his authority alone, even if Republicans lose control of Congress in November and if Democrats were to oppose the continuation of US operations against the country.
Rubio also briefly addressed Trump’s meeting with Delcy Rodriguez, the interim Venezuelan president, who last night posed for a friendly photo with Trump at a Manhattan hotel only miles from where her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, was incarcerated.
“It was a short meeting, but it was a very important meeting,” Rubio said.

articles.title_orig: Son of Israeli ambassador to US critically injured in West Bank ramming attack
articles.title_zh: Son of Israeli ambassador to US critically injured in West Bank ramming attack
articles.content_orig:
The son of Israeli Ambassador to the US Yechiel Leiter was critically injured in a ramming attack in the occupied West Bank on Wednesday afternoon, according to regional authorities, one day before Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s scheduled speech at the United Nations.
Neria Leiter, a reserve soldier manning a checkpoint near the settlement of Beit Horon, was rushed to a hospital in Jerusalem, according to emergency response services.
“Neria needs a miracle,” Leiter said in a statement on social media. “I believe in the power of prayer, and I believe that when the people of Israel unite, miracles happen.”
The driver of the car, 29-year-old Mahmoud Muhammad Mahmoud Suleiman, a Palestinian from the nearby village of Beit Ur al-Tahta, was shot and killed at the scene of the attack, according to the Palestinian Ministry of Health.
Hamas praised the attack in a statement Wednesday, describing it as a “natural response” to Israeli actions in the West Bank and Jerusalem. The militant group in the Gaza Strip called for increased resistance against Israel but did not claim responsibility for the attack.
Leiter’s elder son, 39-year-old Moshe Yedidya Leiter, was killed fighting in Gaza in November 2023 in the first weeks of the war triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel the month before.
The ramming attack occurred just days after a shooting in the West Bank on the eve of the Jewish high holiday of Yom Kippur. On Sunday morning, Netanel Shukrun, a father of six from the settlement of Alei Zahav, was shot and killed while bathing at a natural spring in the West Bank as part of the holiday customs. Shukrun’s 16-year-old son credited his father with saving his life when he shouted out a warning to take cover.
The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) arrested the suspected shooter at a hospital near the West Bank city of Ramallah, the military said Sunday. Far-right National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir called for the death penalty in the case under a new law applying capital punishment to terrorism and nationalistic murders.
After the shooting, Lt. Gen. Eyal Zamir, the IDF chief of staff, said: “The IDF is on high alert, deployed and prepared with soldiers reinforced across all sectors, including throughout the fast. Our mission is clear and ongoing — to thwart terrorism, act decisively against every threat, and protect the citizens of the State of Israel.”
Since October 7, 2023, Israel has carried out waves of widescale military operations in the West Bank intended to target what officials view as centers of terrorist activity. The operations have led to the displacement of tens of thousands of Palestinians across the territory and military raids into Palestinian villages.
“Terrorism currently in Judea and Samaria is at its lowest level in decades,” Defense Minister Israel Katz said in early September, using the biblical name for the West Bank, “and we will take all necessary steps to prevent terrorism from rearing its head again.”
This is a developing story and will be updated.

articles.title_orig: Rebalancing of trade with China 'existential' for EU, Commissioner Séjourné tells Euronews
articles.title_zh: Rebalancing of trade with China 'existential' for EU, Commissioner Séjourné tells Euronews
articles.content_orig:
Rebalancing of trade with China 'existential' for EU, Commissioner Séjourné tells Euronews
The EU Industry Commissioner warned that the EU will consider using punitive trade measures if Beijing does not rebalance the trade deficit, which costs the bloc thousands of jobs every week.
The European Union "urgently" needs to act quickly to rebalance its "unsustainable" trade relationship with China, Commission Executive Vice-President for Prosperity and Industrial Strategy, Stéphane Séjourné, told Euronews, stressing that significant job losses are at stake.
Recent customs data showed the gap between the bloc's imports from China and exports to China, the trade deficit, ran at more than €1 billion a day in July.
"This trade rebalancing is becoming existential for Europeans," Séjourné said on Euronews' interview programme The Europe Conversation.
"Today we're losing thousands of jobs every week," he noted, adding that the EU already lost 250,000 industrial jobs last year. These were particularly concentrated in energy-intensive sectors and automotive supply chains. "It's urgent that we act, and urgent that we rebalance."
The EU, meanwhile, began crucial negotiations with Beijing in June this year, and has set a looming October deadline for concrete, "credible" outcomes. This will culminate in a high-stakes visit by EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič to Beijing on 8 and 9 October, where Brussels is hoping to secure commitments from China that it will curb exports to the EU.
"The European Commission has put forward a proposal to the Chinese side to discuss this sector by sector and look at how we can rebalance things," Séjourné said. "This imbalance isn't sustainable, not for China or for the EU."
However, so far, Beijing has been resisting calls from the Europeans, pushing back against calls for voluntary export curbs.
The EU Industry Commissioner said that negotiation and discussion will be "given a chance," but that the Commission has been clear on the consequences of talks not producing the results.
"Trade defence tools are on the table," he warned. "Today we need credibility in how we use these tools, and we won't hesitate to use them to rebalance things."
Tools currently on the table include anti-dumping duties and tariffs against unfair subsidies (in industries such as electric vehicles and solar panels).
But Brussels is walking a tightrope when it comes to defending the EU market, as Chinese retaliation could see the country restrict exports of rare earths, essential to several of the EU's key industries, including defence.
The EU will also be keeping its eye on talks between Washington and Beijing. Chinese President Xi Jinping is landing in the United States for a three-day summit with US President Donald Trump, which is set to cover issues ranging from trade to AI and rare earths.
The outcome of these talks between the two economic superpowers could directly affect Europe's economic interests, Séjourné explained.
"We need a constructive dialogue between China and the United States. As we saw last year, the trade escalation between Washington and Beijing on these issues could spark a trade war, one that could even affect the European economy."
Last year, an explosive tit-for-tat trade war saw the US and China hike tariffs on each other's goods to dizzying heights. At the peak of this battle, the US imposed 145% tariffs on Chinese imports, while Beijing's retaliatory duties reached 125%.
For Europe, a trade war between the US and China hits hard, as astronomical tariffs on China inevitably lead to the diversion of Chinese goods from the US to the EU.
On the agenda this week in the US will be the looming expiration of the trade truce, due to expire on 10 November.
"I hope this dialogue can be constructive, that an agreement can be reached, and that the situation can be stabilised," Séjourné concluded.

articles.title_orig: Former NASA chief sounds alarm on China’s lunar “exploration” plans
articles.title_zh: Former NASA chief sounds alarm on China’s lunar “exploration” plans
articles.content_orig:
In a forthcoming memoir, former US politician and NASA Administrator Bill Nelson offers a blistering assessment of China, saying the United States must do all it can to retain its leadership in space exploration.
“Beijing’s intended strategy is to dominate the high ground of the twenty-first century,” writes Nelson in Space Odyssey, a book to be published by Harper Horizon in January 2027.
A former Congressman and Senator from Florida, Nelson served as a mission specialist on a space shuttle flight in 1986 and later as NASA administrator from May 2021 to January 2025 under President Biden. The book largely focuses on his space policy work in Congress and his tenure as NASA’s leader.
Nelson recounts how in early 2023, NASA assisted the US military when a Chinese spy balloon began traversing the United States. With its experience in using balloons to map the stratosphere and model atmospheric currents, NASA provided information on how to shoot the balloon down without endangering anyone on the ground.
He argues that the balloon saga offered further affirmation that the United States was enmeshed in a high-stakes competition with China for the high ground.
“What many Americans first registered as a balloon violating our airspace was really a warning that the next great rivalry will not be fought on land or sea but the skies above us and even beyond our atmosphere,” he writes. “The episode was also a window into the new space race that is swiftly approaching its most urgent phase, with the stakes even higher than the Cold War contest.”
Nelson has long been wary of China as a threat to the United States, noting his concerns about technology theft from the West. Unlike his predecessor under a Democratic president—former astronaut Charlie Bolden, who served as NASA leader under President Obama—Nelson supported the Wolf Amendment, which strictly limits cooperation between NASA and China’s space program.

articles.title_orig: Trump plans grand spectacle for potentially tense Xi talks
articles.title_zh: Trump plans grand spectacle for potentially tense Xi talks
articles.content_orig:
When Chinese leader Xi Jinping visits Washington this week, he will be sitting down with President Donald Trump in a vastly different position than the last time the two men met face-to-face in the United States nearly a decade ago.
At that 2017 summit at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort China was lagging America on multiple fronts and vulnerable to the tech and trade frictions Trump would unleash on it in the coming year.
Now, Xi arrives at the helm of a country that’s transformed.
The world’s second largest economy has emerged as a tech heavyweight. Home-grown tech talent is spurring Chinese AI models ever closer to Silicon Valley’s frontier. Beijing-based space firms are launching and landing reuseable rockets with their sights on global champion SpaceX. Companies from energy to AI, robots and memory chips have launched blockbuster stock debuts over the past year.
China’s manufacturing juggernaut racked up a $1.2 trillion global trade surplus last year, due in part to surging demand for its electric vehicles, solar panels and chips. Its grip on the supply chains for some exports – especially rare earths – has given Beijing unique leverage over Washington and Trump’s “America First” trade war.
And at a moment when the US is antagonizing allies and has yet to find a way to end its war on Iran that’s destabilizing the global economy, Xi has been burnishing China’s image as a responsible and dependable global leader.
Throughout policy circles in Beijing, there is a consensus: gone are the days when the US could make one-directional demands of China.
“China is far more confident than nine years ago and what’s even more important is that today China has found an effective way to keep the US in check,” said Wu Xinbo, dean of the Institute of International Studies at Shanghai’s Fudan University, who advises the government on foreign policy.
“Washington has to treat Beijing with more equality, respect and this relationship has to be more and more reciprocal.”
That doesn’t mean the stakes are low for Xi as he arrives in Washington for an expected three-day stay.
The Chinese leader is banking on China’s high-tech transformation to inject momentum into a slowing economy. Maintaining “constructive strategic stability” – an ambition the two sides agreed to during a meeting in Beijing in May – could help ensure frictions or conflict with the US don’t get in the way.
But buoyed by China’s growing global and technological clout, Xi will also be presenting to the US a new reality: while Beijing wants a stable relationship with the US, its rise doesn’t depend on it.
In a bullish editorial in party mouthpiece the People’s Daily on Wednesday that helps illustrate this confidence, China’s ambassador to the US warned that Taiwan and human rights are “red lines” for Beijing that cannot be crossed.
“China’s sovereignty, security, and development interests must not be violated. The four red lines concerning the Taiwan issue, democracy and human rights, China’s political system and development path, and its right to development must not be challenged,” Xie Feng wrote.
For Xi, a key source of that confidence has been China’s ability to diversify trade away from the US market and build out its technological self-sufficiency – two mandates sharpened by pressures on China from the first Trump administration.
Beijing has funneled vast financing and political will toward building its own technology in cutting-edge sectors – like robotics, AI, biotech, space, new energy and chips – and applying that tech into industry.
The fruits of that growth, however, are not spread evenly. Youth unemployment hit a recent high last month. Hundreds of millions of workers rely on the gig economy, such as delivering food or driving ride-share cars for their primary work. Consumption lags, local governments struggle under debt and a huge property sector crisis rumbles on.
People from all walks of life in China will readily tell you that the economy is just not doing as good as it used to be. But alongside this, there is often a sense of pride that the country has been able to rise as a tech power, even in the face of US-imposed restrictions.
Look no further than the case of Huawei, the Chinese tech giant blacklisted by the first Trump administration. In recent days Chinese tech vloggers have been gleefully posting videos about Apple’s much-hyped release of its first foldable phone. They point out that Huawei’s own foldable model came out seven years ago.
Days ahead of Xi’s visit to the US, Huawei also announced that its next generation of Ascend AI chips would be released ahead of schedule next year, signaling progress in what has been a crucial bottleneck for China in AI development.
“We cannot accept a destiny where we cannot control our fate being determined by others in terms of willingness to sell chips to China or not,” Huawei rotating chairman Eric Xu said earlier this month.
And while the American public is largely pessimistic about the development of AI, their peers in China are more focused on how it might impact their day-to-day lives. Job displacement is a concern, but there’s also a sense there is an opportunity to be seized – and that the ruling Communist Party, with its tight control over society, won’t let the technology spin out of control.
Xi is heading to the US in the middle of an explosion of conversation about the risks of AI, including from Chinese models. Trump has said the country can’t slow development for safety, because it must focus on beating China.
That puts the spotlight on a key aim from Xi and his delegation: to dissuade the US from more tech restrictions that further could limit Chinese firms’ access to American technology or markets.
China wants to see “greater predictability in the economic and technology relationship” and a “stronger political commitment to prevent sensitive issues — especially Taiwan and technology restrictions — from destabilizing the overall relationship,” according to Sun Chenghao, a senior fellow at Tsinghua University’s Center for International Security and Strategy in Beijing.
But this is also where the shifting balance of power between China and the US comes in.
Both sides know that new restrictions – if seen by Beijing as too aggressive – could reignite the conflict that led their economies to the brink of full decoupling last year.
The truce that ended that round of their trade war was reached only after Beijing threatened a massive expansion of export controls on strategically critical rare earths, in response to a US move that would have vastly expanded the number of blacklisted Chinese firms.
That truce will likely be extended this week – and both sides will be wary of pushing the other too far in a situation where “nobody wins, because it’s equally matched,” according to Kurt Tong, managing partner at The Asia Group advisory firm.
“In the economic space, there isn’t really any superior player … because of the equally matched leverage aspects, the two sides are pulling back from actions that cost them to execute,” said Tong, who formerly served as the US consul general of Hong Kong.
Now, Trump “looks at Xi Jinping and sees a counterpart as opposed to someone to wrestle into submission,” he said.
China is now seen more positively than the US in most of 36 countries surveyed in a new Pew Research poll published in July. Xi even edged out Trump in winning people’s confidence, the pollsters found.
These changes come not just alongside a shake-up of the role of the US on the global stage, but a shift in China’s ability to wield soft power. People around the world are using Chinese AI models for their businesses and driving Chinese EVs. Viral cultural exports like the Labubu plushy and Chinese dramas, as well as the online Chinamaxxing trend have driven interest and tourism in China.

articles.title_orig: America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
articles.title_zh: America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
articles.content_orig:
America Is Losing the Ability to Train Tomorrow’s China Experts. The Trump-Xi Summit Can Help.
Long-standing educational programs such as Fulbright, Boren, and the Critical Language Scholarship are all suspended. A leader-level deal could bring them back and protect the students who take part.
- Rosie LevineExecutive Director of the U.S.-China Education Trust
- Rush DoshiCFR ExpertC.V. Starr Senior Fellow for Asia Studies and Director of the China Strategy Initiative
Derk Bodde set out for Beijing in 1948 expecting to spend a quiet year translating an esoteric work of Chinese philosophy. Instead, as the first recipient of the newly created Fulbright fellowship in China, he found himself an eyewitness to the Chinese Communist Party’s takeover, and his account of what he saw became a rare firsthand record for policymakers, academics, and the American public. When China closed to foreign contact for the next quarter-century, Bodde’s expertise didn’t just remain useful: it was irreplaceable.
Bodde’s story is a clear example of the ways in which in-country research is a proven and often indispensable tool to strengthen American expertise of foreign countries—and not only with friendly nations. But as Presidents Donald Trump and Xi Jinping prepare to meet tomorrow in Washington, DC, only around two thousand Americans are studying in China, down from fifteen thousand a decade ago, and the public and private ecosystem that once supported deep American study of China is collapsing precisely when it is needed most.
That decline is due both to funding cuts and legitimate concerns that students may face risks of arbitrary detention in China. Currently, two American academics have been designated as wrongfully detained after traveling to China for academic purposes, creating risks that must be addressed by Beijing. Such cases are rare—the vast majority of Americans who study in China do so without incident—but they are real, and their chilling effect reaches far beyond the individuals involved. At the upcoming summit, Presidents Trump and President Xi should elevate specific programs like Fulbright into leader-level deliverables, with President Xi’s high-profile support for them at the summit providing implicit assurances that participants will not face undue risks from China’s security services.
This approach has some precedent. Exchange programs sometimes receive broad protections from leaders. Indeed, even at the height of the Cold War, the United States established the International Research and Exchanges Board (IREX) in 1968 as a formalized, bilateral academic exchange mechanism, sending generations of American Sovietologists into the Soviet Union, even as the two countries remained locked in rivalry. IREX and its successors, including the Committee on Scholarly Communication with the People’s Republic of China, which managed similar style exchanges with China before diplomatic normalization, were established to lend U.S. government protection to academic exchanges deemed essential to the national interest.
By contrast, the China programs that built a generation of expertise are now defunct. The Fulbright Program has been suspended in China since 2020, partly over risks that participating students and researchers might be detained by China. Alongside Fulbright, less well-known but essential U.S. government–funded programs specifically designed to encourage greater foreign area expertise in government have been suspended to mainland China, including the Boren Awards, the Critical Language Scholarship, the National Security Language Initiative for Youth (NSLI-Y), and more.
At home, the area studies infrastructure in U.S. universities that was built in the 1950s, including the National Resource Centers, Title VI funding, and Foreign Language and Area Studies (FLAS) fellowships, has been gutted amid cuts at the Department of Education. In recent weeks, new unclear federal restrictions on higher education’s ties to China have pushed some universities to conclude that even nonsensitive academic engagement—undergraduate study abroad included—carries too much risk: the University of North Carolina is the latest institution to pull down its study abroad program.
Critics of travel to China argue that Taiwan offers a safer alternative for Mandarin language study, and that the extent of state surveillance makes the risk of visiting China not worth the potential benefits. But Taiwan’s educational opportunities, while excellent, cannot fully substitute for the loss of access to China’s economy, society, and culture.
America needs a much deeper supply of China experts to handle a fast-changing relationship. In closed-door meetings compiled for the U.S.-China Education Trust’s 2026 report, America’s China Talent Challenge, stakeholders across the U.S. government, business, and academia described how their sectors depend on American expertise to interpret China’s actions—from geopolitics and security, to trade and supply chains—and to keep the United States competitive. The working group concluded that China expertise must be considered a national resource.
As Trump and Xi meet in Washington, progress on people-to-people diplomacy may be less challenging than in other domains. But both sides can take steps to improve the situation.
First, the Trump administration should negotiate with Beijing to elevate specific programs, from named legacy programs—including the Fulbright, Boren, Critical Language Scholarship, and NSLI-Y—to new initiatives, into summit deliverables. President Xi’s endorsement of these programs would provide implicit protection for those students who participate in them. President Trump could privately push to formalize assurances that participants will face no risks from China’s security services. And to make that gesture credible, Beijing should release detained academics.
Second, in tandem with these negotiations, the United States should reverse cuts to funding programs, which are in many cases entirely unrelated to China. The area studies infrastructure built nearly eighty years ago, to include National Resource Centers, Title VI funding, and FLAS fellowships, has been gutted and should be restored. Congress should also fund new programs, purpose-built for today’s U.S.-China relationship. Scrutiny of university ties to China is in some cases warranted, but it should be scoped so that nonsensitive academic engagement, such as undergraduate study abroad and language programs, are able to proceed with appropriate safeguards.
To some, these proposals may seem unrealistic. But they are rooted in history and pragmatism. Washington has long had educational programs in countries with competitors and adversaries. Those programs were often sustained by leader-level understandings that they would be insulated from competitive dynamics in the relationship. Improving mutual understanding is inherently valuable. For both Washington and Beijing, it also reduces the risk of miscalculation. If the next generation of policymakers has no China experience, both countries will suffer.
A United States that no longer trains people who can read Chinese primary sources, sit in Chinese classrooms, or track policy implementation on the ground is hardly more secure and is substantially less capable. Rebuilding China expertise is not an act of goodwill toward Beijing. It is a hard-nosed investment in the United States’ atrophying ability to understand and compete with its most consequential rival.
The United States and China have few bright spots in the bilateral relationship, and fewer still that could be elevated into summit deliverables. Naming and insulating a handful of exchange programs from political and security pressures is in fact one of the most straightforward areas for cooperation that exists between the two countries.
This work represents the views solely of the author(s). The Council on Foreign Relations is an independent, nonpartisan membership organization, think

articles.title_orig: J.J. McCarthy, Mac Jones, Jimmy Garoppolo and 4 other QBs who could help teams in need - The Athletic
articles.title_zh: J.J. McCarthy, Mac Jones, Jimmy Garoppolo and 4 other QBs who could help teams in need - The Athletic
articles.content_orig:
Five plays into the 2026 NFL season, we saw the first starting quarterback go down.
The Seattle Seahawks' Sam Darnold suffered a glute injury against the New England Patriots, and just like that, Drew Lock was leading the defending Super Bowl champs to a comeback victory on Opening Night.
It wouldn't take much longer for more starting quarterbacks to fall.
Less than 10 minutes into his Vikings debut in Week 1, Kyler Murray was knocked out with a concussion. Week 2 saw three recent first-round quarterbacks succumb to injury: Chicago's Caleb Williams and Washington's Jayden Daniels, the first two picks of the 2024 NFL Draft, followed by the Giants' Jaxson Dart — and each injury seemingly worse than the next.
Along with the Atlanta Falcons, who were forced to start Cooper Rush the first two games ahead of either Tua Tagovailoa or Michael Penix Jr., it's fair to say that the starting-quarterback injury epidemic is already raging after two weeks. Nearly 20% of the league has been forced to play backup QBs, with almost 90% of the regular season still remaining.
Backups clearly matter. Brock Purdy missed almost half the 2025 regular season, but Mac Jones helped keep the 49ers afloat. When C.J. Stroud missed three games last season, Texans backup Davis Mills went 3-0 in his place, keeping them in the playoff race. But when Patrick Mahomes got hurt, the drop-off to Gardner Minshew — and later Chris Oladokun — was too steep for the Chiefs to survive.
Some teams, we're finding out, have protected their most important assets better than others. Here's how we'd rank the six teams that have needed to dip into their QB reserves:
6) Tua Tagovailoa/Michael Penix Jr./Cooper Rush/Jack Strand, Atlanta Falcons
Who's the starter? Who's the backup? It's often not a pretty situation when those two questions aren't followed by easy answers.
The Falcons have the toughest situation of the lot right now, even with the most theoretical options. Tagovailoa was nominally the starter until he got hurt; Penix, the logical replacement, couldn't go the first two weeks.
That left the reins to Rush, who struggled in Baltimore last season and who did little in his two starts this season in leading the Falcons to an 0-2 start. Strand, the Division-II prospect who had an encouraging preseason, replaced Rush in Week 2 and threw a pick-6 on his first NFL pass attempt.
Clearly the hope is that the often-injured Penix can step in now, having been named Atlanta's Week 3 starter, and run with the job. The Falcons have little other hope, short of (the also often-injured) Tagovailoa returning to action.
Until proven otherwise, Kevin Stefanski has the same issue in Atlanta that he had in Cleveland: quarterback uncertainty.
5) Jameis Winston, New York Giants
With Jaxson Dart now ruled out for the season, the Giants are in a really tough spot, with no young quarterback to prepare in the wings. Winston has a wealth of experience, with 89 career starts, but as Monday's replacement performance showed, his play can be a wild experience.
Winston struggled against the Rams and has been a turnover machine in his career, with 141 of them (114 INTs, 27 lost fumbles) in 109 career outings. He's had a five-pick game and a three-fumble game. Winston also has five career 400-yard games and two five-TD, no-INT performances. You really never know what you're going to get any given week.
Head coach John Harbaugh has to find another option in case he gets too much bad Winston, with only Jake Haener currently on the practice squad. Some have floated a J.J. McCarthy trade to the Giants, but would that throw only more gas on the fire?
4) Tyson Bagent/Case Keenum, Chicago Bears
This pairing could arguably be higher on the list, but Bagent's concussion (which might have come on the final play Sunday) could keep him out of Monday night's game against the Philadelphia Eagles, which would give Keenum his first start — and his first regular-season action — since 2023.
Bagent has barely seen the field since Caleb Williams was drafted, but he started four games in 2023 and replaced Williams for the final two drives Sunday. His body of work is incomplete, but Bagent possesses intriguing skills and it wouldn't be shocking if he led a team at starter level for a stretch.
It's unclear how long Williams will be out, but for the first time since he came to Chicago, the Bears will have to lean on his replacements.
3) Drew Lock/Jalen Milroe, Seattle Seahawks
Lock came in cold in Week 1 and did just enough to help the Seahawks win, settling down after a few shaky patches. Then he came out guns blazing in Week 2, throwing for three TDs. Would you believe that Lock leads the NFL in passer rating through two games? He entered the season completing fewer than 60% of his career passes but is sitting at 72.7% in 2026.
If Lock, who turns 30 in November, can continue to fill in ably for the injured Darnold, it's not a stretch to think he could follow the Geno Smith post-30 path of earning his way back into a starting lineup, perhaps as a bridge option for a team that drafts a higher-round QB next spring. It appears that Lock has worked out some of the recklessness in his game and is becoming more dependable.
Milroe remains a curiosity with strong physical skills, but he's still virtually unknown. His best shot might be to continue working behind the scenes and vie for Lock's QB2 spot next season.
2) Carson Wentz/J.J. McCarthy, Minnesota Vikings
Wentz might be known in some circles as a bust, or as the guy whose team went on to win a Super Bowl after he got hurt. Even still, he's carved out a career for himself as an able QB2, willing and ready to jump into the fire. He did so early against the Packers when Kyler Murray got hurt, leading the Vikings to a 12-point comeback in the game's final 20 minutes. Then Wentz turned in a solid, turnover-free effort in his Week 2 start against the Bears, leading Minnesota to a shocking 9-3 win and a 2-0 start to the season.
Not bad for a guy who wasn't even part of the Vikings' starting derby in camp. His outing vs. the Bears marked 11 straight seasons with at least one start for Wentz. He'll take a seat again with Murray expected to start in Week 3, but Wentz's contributions can't be forgotten.
McCarthy, who lost the starting battle to Murray, remains an enigma. He's under contract through 2027 with a 2028 option, but the path back to being relevant for this team appears longer and more windy now.
1) Marcus Mariota/Athan Kaliakmanis,
Mariota is in some ways the gold standard of backup quarterbacks, along with the 49ers' Jones. With 82 career starts, Mariota has more experience than many current starters. He stepped in ably for Jayden Daniels in Sunday's loss to the Cowboys, looking sharp, and was competitive during Daniels' two missed stints last season.
With Daniels expected to miss 4-6 weeks with his latest left elbow injury, Mariota will be thrust back onto the saddle as he approaches his 33rd birthday. The biggest benefit is that he can run the same offense Daniels did, with little tweaking necessary.
The rookie Kaliakmanis had a strong preseason, receiving extra reps when Mariota's knee injury flared up and impressing the team with his arm talent and moxie.

articles.title_orig: 6 people killed in bear attacks in Siberia, as official warns one town is "under siege"
articles.title_zh: 6 people killed in bear attacks in Siberia, as official warns one town is "under siege"
articles.content_orig:
At least six people have been killed in bear attacks in Russia's vast Siberian region of Krasnoyarsk in a month, prosecutors said Wednesday, as an official in a neighboring region reported bears had put one town "under siege."
Prosecutors said they opened a probe into criminal negligence, accusing local officials of failing to control bear numbers.
Russia's brown bear population has more than doubled since 1990, from around 130,000 to almost 308,000 in 2026, according to Russia's natural resources ministry.
While the number of bear attacks across Russia has remained constant at around 20 to 30 a year, according to the ministry, local media and officials have expressed alarm about the rising numbers. At least 14 people have been killed in bear attacks across Russia since the start of the year, according to a tally by The Moscow Times .
Despite numerous warnings, local officials "failed to take measures to regulate the predator population or prevent them from appearing in areas inhabited by people," the Investigative Committee of Russia's sparsely populated Krasnoyarsk and Khakassia regions said on its website.
The bodies of two pensioners were found mauled in a forest near the remote town of Podtyosovo earlier this month, followed by the death of a 40-year-old factory worker who walked through the forest on Sept. 6, according to local media.
Earlier this month, two people were killed while foraging for wild berries in a remote forest on the banks of the Lena River, the Moscow Times reported .
"One person managed to escape and report the incident," the regional branch of Russia's Interior Ministry said, according to the outlet.
A 39-year-old logger guarding machinery was killed by a bear in the forest early Wednesday, investigators said.
The deputy head of the neighboring Khakassia region, Dmitry Buchenik, said Wednesday that the forest town of Abaza — home to around 10,000 people — was surrounded by bears "on all sides."
"It was an alarming night in Abaza. The taiga town is effectively under siege by bears," he said.
"Some of the animals were chased off, but three were killed (one of them was huge)," he added.
Unverified social media videos purported to show a bear swimming across a river beside the town, while another showed a group of three bears leaping across a road in front of cars.
Russia's emergency ministry says bears flee in the vast majority of encounters with humans.
Earlier this year, officials said three members of a family, including a child, were injured by a polar bear in a rare attack in the far north of Siberia.
