articles.title_orig: Scientists warn super El Nino could cause 450,000 deaths: Should we worry?
articles.title_zh: Scientists warn super El Nino could cause 450,000 deaths: Should we worry?
articles.content_orig:
Scientists warn super El Nino could cause 450,000 deaths: Should we worry?
Global South countries will be worst affected by the phenomenon sweeping the planet from June to February.
The record global heat caused by this year’s powerful “super El Nino” could cause nearly half a million excess deaths worldwide by early next year, according to a report (PDF) published by the global research collaboration, Climate Impact Lab, on Wednesday.
So what does the report reveal, how has climate change supercharged the effects of El Nino and should we all be really worried?
- list 1 of 3UN warns El Nino could be ‘off the charts’, strongest in decades
- list 2 of 3Global ocean temperatures hit record high as El Nino intensifies
- list 3 of 3El Nino set to be most intense ‘for over a century’: UK forecasters
Climate Impact Lab (CIL)’s report has found that as many as 451,000 more heat-related deaths between June this year and the end of February 2027 could be caused by the effects of El Nino, than the number expected in an average year.
The study’s authors came to their projections after researching the relationship between temperature and excess mortality in 24,378 regions, taking local climate and vulnerability into account.
They combined those findings with temperature forecasts to estimate excess deaths which could arise from heat caused by El Nino compared with the 1996-2025 average.
Their methodology will be published in a peer-reviewed journal.
The number of extremely hot days is likely to rise by 44 percent compared with normal years, according to the report, titled, “451,000 at Risk: Where Action Can Save Lives During the Super El Nino”.
The researchers described this year’s El Nino as a “postcard from the future”, ushering in temperatures that will become the new normal in just a few decades.
It recommended that emergency response efforts should be directed to high-priority regions to tackle heat-related mortality in the coming months.
CIL’s Adaptation Inventory recommends implementing a number of measures to help vulnerable populations cope with extreme heat, including issuing heat warnings, increasing the number of staff at medical facilities during the hottest periods, establishing cooling centres where people can shelter and implementing protections for outdoor workers.
“This report allows decision-makers to see exactly where emergency actions can be taken now to save tens of thousands of lives in the coming months,” said Michael Greenstone, economist at the University of Chicago and cofounder of CIL.
El Nino is the period of time during which the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean heats up to at least 0.5 degrees Celsius (0.9 degrees Fahrenheit) above average temperatures. It takes place every few years and is part of a natural climate cycle that alternates between a warm phase – El Nino – and a cool phase, known as La Nina.
During El Nino, the warmer ocean water can drive major changes in global weather patterns.
Scientists and meteorologists classify El Nino as “super” when ocean surface temperatures reach or exceed 2C (3.6F) for a few months. The current El Nino reached 2.7C last month, and some forecasts say it could rise to 4C when it peaks somewhere between November and December.
Why is it so bad this year?
The way El Nino develops depends a lot on “how the atmosphere and the ocean are behaving”, Akshay Deoras, senior research scientist at the University of Reading’s National Centre for Atmospheric Science & Department of Meteorology, told Al Jazeera.
Early in the year generally, “you get winds blowing towards Indonesia and these winds pile up warm water over there. But sometimes, if the winds weaken or the wind pattern is reversed, then that’s when you get strong winds from the Indonesia side, and that leads to a lot of transport of warm water”, Deoras explained.
This warm water then heads towards the eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, resulting in El Nino.
“This year, we have really seen these strong winds from Indonesia blowing in the spring season, and they help to transport a large amount of hot water or let’s say warm water, and that’s why we have a super El Nino.”
What effects will it have?
Despite its unprecedented strength, it remains unclear what effects this year’s super El Nino will have on weather around the world.
“Scientists are still assessing whether the impacts will be in proportion to its magnitude, but we are already seeing expected effects worldwide,” said Adam Scaife, head of long-range forecasting at the United Kingdom’s Met Office.
“Historical evidence shows that El Nino can significantly alter global rainfall patterns,” the Met Office said in a statement.
Regions that often experience reduced rainfall during this period include parts of Central and northern South America, the western Pacific and areas affected by the Indian summer monsoon.
Other areas, including Southern Africa, may face an increased risk of drought.
El Nino also reduces tropical cyclone activity in the Atlantic, with the Met Office adding that no hurricanes have been observed yet this year.
The disruption to rainfall can have severe consequences on global food supplies as agriculture suffers and natural food-growing and harvesting seasons are altered.
Why could El Nino cause so many excess deaths?
The main thing that El Nino does “is it just dumps a lot of heat into the atmosphere and we know that this heat and high temperatures basically supercharges extreme rainfall and weather events”, said Deoras.
A super El Nino not only increases the frequency of these events, but also amplifies their intensity and severity, meaning that there is a “general expectation that we would get more of these extreme weather events across the globe over the next couple of months, and unfortunately, that could translate into a lot of deaths,” said Deoras.
How is climate change involved in this?
Friederike Otto, professor of climate science at Imperial College London, said that climate change has worsened the impact of El Nino around the world.
“El Nino is likely to bring higher global temperatures and extreme weather impacts in the months ahead, and climate change will further exacerbate these impacts, as the underlying heat driven by fossil fuel emissions continues to push global temperatures higher,” said Otto.
“However, while El Nino patterns are a natural phenomenon that come and go, climate change does not and will only continue to worsen unless we take much faster action globally to move away from fossil fuels.”
Which countries will be worst affected and why?
The Climate Impact Lab report warns that countries in the Global South will bear the heaviest burden of the excessive heat.
The country likely to suffer the most excess heat-related deaths is Nigeria with 31,400, followed by Indonesia with 19,300 and Sudan with 17,600.
Heat in Africa’s Sahel region, including Niger and Chad as well as Nigeria and Sudan, is likely to cause an additional 66,800 deaths.
The researchers also predict that the Philippines, Vietnam, Thailand and Cambodia will suffer an additional 19,400 deaths combined.
The number of excess deaths could climb higher if El Nino extends further into next year, with key areas of the Northern Hemisphere, including India and Pakistan, especially vulnerable during their summer months.
Tom Burke, cofounder and director of the climate change think tank E3G, agreed that the Global South would be disproportionately affected.
“Coping with the additional stresses caused by El Nino is harder on countries that have weaker institutions. So the poorer a country it is, the weaker institutions it has,” he told Al Jazeera.
Countries of the Global North, by contrast, have “a whole variety of institutions to respond to these kinds of stresses: fire departments, health systems, etc. They have a quite complex set of institutions to respond to events like this”.
Deoras said added that “it’s quite difficult to” assume that El Nino will impact the Southern Hemisphere

articles.title_orig: Galaxy Tab S12+ and S12 Ultra specs leak - here's what will be upgraded - GSMArena.com news
articles.title_zh: Galaxy Tab S12+ and S12 Ultra specs leak - here's what will be upgraded - GSMArena.com news
articles.content_orig:
There has been a slow trickle of leaks for the Galaxy Tab S12+ and Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra. Now, WinFuture has fully opened the tap and... not much came out. The Tab S12 slates will change a few things from their predecessors, but the upgrades are pretty sparse.
Both tablets will be powered by the Dimensity 9500, which replaces a Dimensity 9400+ on the Tab S11 Ultra and a Dimensity 9300+ on the Tab S10+. Why no “plus” chipset this year? Well, MediaTek never released a 9500+ – there is a Dimensity 9600M, but that doesn’t change enough to get a “plus” tag. There’s also the Dimensity 9600 Pro, but that was only just announced. So, Dimensity 9500 it is.
As you may have noticed, the Galaxy Tab S12+ only has one camera on its back – it’s a 13MP wide module. The Tab S10+ did have a dual-camera setup with an 8MP ultra-wide, but Samsung dropped it for some reason.
The Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra keeps both the 12MP wide and the 8MP ultra-wide modules, plus there is a 12MP selfie. The 14.6” display of the Ultra has a notch to accommodate the selfie camera, while the 12.4” display of the “plus” slate doesn’t need a notch (it has thicker bezels instead).
The Tab S12 Ultra will measure 5.1mm thick (same as before) and will have the same 11,600mAh battery with support for 45W charging. The Tab S12+, however, is getting a new 10,600mAh battery (a minor upgrade from the 10,090mAh of the Tab S10+) with the same 45W charging. The new “plus” slate will be 0.3mm thinner than its predecessor and will measure 5.3mm.
Roland Quandt posted EPREL labels for the two tablets. They show that the batteries are rated for 1,200 charge cycles (no change for the Ultra, but the old “plus” had a 2,000 cycle battery). Also, battery life for the new Ultra has decreased to 88:54h, compared to 94:51h for the 2025 Ultra. As for the “plus” models, the Tab S12+ will last 80:34h, which is an increase from the 73:44h for the Tab S10+. We doubt the 510mAh extra in the battery made that much of a difference, so it’s probably thanks to the more efficient chipset (and possibly screen too).
EPREL labels: Tab S12+ (Wi-Fi) • Tab S12+ (5G) • Tab S12 Ultra (Wi-Fi) • Tab S12 Ultra (5G)
The battery life ratings for the Wi-Fi and 5G versions of the two tablets are the same. Like before, the slates have a low E rating for drop resistance, an average C rating for repairability and an IP68 dust and water resistance rating.
A couple of weeks ago, WinFuture also shared the European prices for the Galaxy Tab S12 Ultra and the Tab S12+. Doubling the storage costs €200, while getting a 5G modem is €150 more. For comparison, a Tab S11 Wi-Fi 12/256GB slate started at €1,340 last year, the 5G version with the same storage was €1,490. In other words, the S12 generation Ultra will be €200 more than its predecessor from last year. There was no Tab S11+ last year, so there is no direct comparison.
By the way, we’ve also seen leaks for the US prices and the Indian prices – those leaks showed price hikes of varying degrees. While not officially confirmed, Samsung is expected to unveil the Galaxy Tab S12 series on October 7.

articles.title_orig: Netanyahu coming to NYC, where Mamdani once vowed to arrest him for war crimes
articles.title_zh: Netanyahu coming to NYC, where Mamdani once vowed to arrest him for war crimes
articles.content_orig:
The months-in-the-making clash between Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Benjamin Netanyahu will come to a head on Thursday when the Israeli prime minister delivers a speech before the U.N. General Assembly in Manhattan.
The two are poised to become the focal point of the annual gathering of the world’s most powerful people, which brings motorcades, gridlock and demonstrations to the city. This year’s event comes with an additional layer of drama: During his mayoral campaign last year, Mamdani threatened to arrest Netanyahu on an International Criminal Court warrant. The mayor later clarified he doesn’t have the authority to arrest the prime minister, but has still called him a “war criminal.”
In a CNN interview released on Tuesday, Mamdani maintained his criticism, saying the warrant against Netanyahu for war crimes and crimes against humanity is “something that should be honored, because what we want to see, and we’ve been talking about this today, is a faith in our politics, a faith in accountability.”
Netanyahu teased his upcoming remarks on Tuesday with a video where he falsely accused the mayor of supporting Hamas and inciting riots against Jewish New Yorkers. He also delivered a direct message to Mamdani. “I'm coming to the U.N.,” he said. “I'm going to tell the truth about our heroic soldiers and I'm going to tell the truth about you.”
Asked about the video, the mayor called Netanyahu the “architect of a horrific genocide against Palestinians” and referenced ongoing Israeli attacks in Gaza.
The NYPD has warned protests are anticipated near the U.N. on Manhattan's East Side throughout the General Assembly. Mamdani has said he won’t attend protests against Netanyahu — noting he would uphold the right to demonstrate peacefully.
Sal Albanese, a former city councilmember who advised Mamdani on public safety, said he believed the mayor could balance the two interests of politics and public safety. Mamdani’s pro-Palestinian activism is a key part of his identity that fueled his election and continued popularity, he said. Similarly, protests are a fixture of the city.
“Netanyahu is obviously going to drive a lot of people on the street to protest,” he said. “As long as they do it peacefully, I don’t think it will be a problem.”
In July, Jewish leaders criticized the mayor for inflaming tensions with his criticism of Israel following the stabbings of a Jewish man and an Asian man on the Upper West Side. The attack occurred days after Mamdani had released a video acknowledging that he did not have the legal authority to order Netanyahu’s arrest. Nevertheless, he said Netanyahu was a “war criminal.”
This is not the first time a New York City mayor has clashed with a foreign leader in town for the General Assembly. In 1995, Mayor Rudy Giuliani directed his Chief of Staff Randy Mastro to ask Yasir Arafat, then the chair of the Palestine Liberation Organization, to leave a Lincoln Center concert. The Clinton administration issued a statement criticizing Giuliani’s actions.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Citizen Injured After Mistakenly Detained by ICE Near Chicago
articles.title_zh: U.S. Citizen Injured After Mistakenly Detained by ICE Near Chicago
articles.content_orig:
EVANSTON, Ill. (WLS) -- An Evanston man was injured when federal immigration agents detained him after mistakenly believing he was someone they were looking for, according to Evanston police and a witness who recorded part of the confrontation. The man was released after agents determined he was a U.S. citizen.
Miguel Olivares said he was taking a break while helping out at El Pueblito Mexican Grill on Howard Street when he noticed vehicles parked outside and a confrontation unfolding.
"It looked like police vehicles until I started hearing, 'I'm a U.S. citizen. I'm a U.S. citizen,'" Olivares said.
Olivares said he then pulled out his phone and began recording.
"They were being rough with him; they had him pinned against the floor, and it looked like one of the agents hit him in the face," Olivares said.
Evanston police said officers were called to the area Sunday morning after someone reported hearing two men arguing. Officers found an unidentified man on the ground with injuries to his head, neck and teeth and called an ambulance, police said.
Police said witnesses told them the men involved appeared to be U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents. Officers later encountered agents nearby who said they were looking for someone who resembled the Evanston man, according to police. The agents determined the man was a U.S. citizen and released him, police said.
The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that the individual in question was "not cooperative" with law enforcement.
Olivares said he and others tried to comfort the man after the encounter.
"He was shooken up. He wasn't really able to talk much. All he said was that he was a U.S. citizen, that he doesn't know why they targeted him," Olivares said.
Nathan Ryan of Sanctuary Evanston said the incident warrants accountability and an investigation into the use of force and the mistaken detention of an Evanston resident.
"The only thing that I can think of that's scarier than federal agents beating up people in the street is federal agents beating up people on the street without repercussions," Ryan said.
Evanston's police chief said she met with the victim in the hospital to make sure he has the support he needs. The identities of the Evanston resident and the federal agents have not been released.
A DHS spokesperson said in a statement: "On September 20, during a targeted enforcement operation in Evanston, Illinois, ICE encountered an individual who resembled the target."
"ICE approached the individual and immediately identified themselves as law enforcement. The individual was given lawful commands but was not cooperative and refused to identify himself."
"ICE officers relied on their training and later left the scene without further incident once the individual finally identified himself."
"ICE has authority for lawful arrests where authorized under 8 USC 1357. Law enforcement officers use 'reasonable suspicion' to investigate immigration status and probable cause to make arrests consistent with the statute and the Fourth Amendment to the U.S. Constitution."
"The Supreme Court has already vindicated us on these practices."
"DHS enforcement operations are highly targeted, and officers do their due diligence."
"We know who we are targeting ahead of time. If and when we do encounter individuals subject to arrest, our law enforcement is trained to ask a series of well-determined questions to determine status and removability."

articles.title_orig: China's Xi will kick off his state visit to Washington with a rare planeside welcome from Trump
articles.title_zh: China's Xi will kick off his state visit to Washington with a rare planeside welcome from Trump
articles.content_orig:
The Latest: China’s Xi to kick off visit to Washington with a rare planeside welcome from Trump
When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington, he’s expected to get a rare greeting from President Donald Trump, who’ll be on the tarmac to welcome his counterpart’s plane instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington on Wednesday, he’s expected to get a rare greeting from President Donald Trump, who'll be on the tarmac to welcome his counterpart’s plane instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House. Trump’s decision to greet Xi shows how far the U.S. president is going to honor China’s leader as he makes his first state visit in more than a decade.
Also, Trump’s AI-fueled vision for a drone port he intends to install atop the new White House ballroom includes missile-bearing unmanned aerial vehicles and gun-toting troops. But what hasn't been previously reported is the presence of a drone port a few hundred feet away, run by the U.S. Secret Service and not the military, which is already quietly operational.
Taiwan is watching closely as Xi and Trump meet and hopes US will keep up its arms sales
As China’s Xi Jinping arrives in Washington to meet with President Trump, Taiwan expressed confidence that U.S. arms sales to the island that Beijing claims as its own will continue — despite China’s pressure.
China has pressed Washington to halt the arms sales, most prominently during a summit in May between Trump and Xi in Beijing. After that meeting, the United States paused the sale of a record-breaking $14 billion package — and Trump described arms sales to Taiwan as a “very good negotiating chip” with China.
Still, the U.S. government and Congress have “repeatedly expressed support for Taiwan’s self-defense capabilities,” Taiwanese Defense Ministry spokesperson Maj. Gen. Chiao Fu-chun told reporters in the southern city of Tainan.
Trump says his ballroom will house a drone port. The Secret Service already has one next door
Trump’s AI-fueled vision for a drone port he intends to install atop the new White House ballroom includes missile-bearing unmanned aerial vehicles and gun-toting troops, ostensibly to protect the 18-acre complex and the nation’s capital.
A few hundred feet away, a drone port, run by the U.S. Secret Service and not the military, is already quietly operational. Equipped with cameras and sensors to scope out potential threats from a bird’s-eye view, the small UAVs stand on alert in four gray weatherproof boxes until deployed at officers’ commands.
The agency is using a model known as “drone as first responder,” deploying speedy unarmed drones from outdoor stations to serve as flying cameras. That model has been adopted by hundreds of police agencies across the U.S., often powered by AI software to help dodge obstacles or track targets.
The existence of the surveillance drones on a Treasury Department building adjacent to the White House complex has not been previously reported, and could undercut Trump’s legal claims that the ballroom construction is necessary “to protect the White House and surrounding region from aerial attacks.”
Xi is en route to Washington
Xi has departed Beijing on Wednesday afternoon local time for a state visit to the U.S., China’s official news agency Xinhua said. Accompanying him on the visit are Xi’s wife Peng Liyuan, China’s ruling Communist Party’s Politburo Standing Committee member Cai Qi and Foreign Minister Wang Yi, it said.
China’s Xi to kick off state visit to Washington with rare planeside welcome from Trump
When Chinese President Xi Jinping arrives in Washington on Wednesday, he’s expected to get a rare greeting from President Donald Trump, who will be on the tarmac to welcome his counterpart’s plane instead of waiting for him to drive up to the White House.
Trump’s decision to greet Xi at Joint Base Andrews shows how far the U.S. president is going to honor China’s leader as he makes his first state visit in more than a decade.
The White House hasn't released many details about Wednesday’s greeting, but Trump is expected to participate in an arrival ceremony at the base with Xi and his wife. The salutation will kick off a three-day visit that’s expected to be saturated with pomp, even by White House standards. The state visit, complete with a formal state dinner at the White House on Thursday, is supposed to reciprocate for the ceremonial grandeur that marked Trump’s May visit to China.
But it’s also a showy patina at a time when tensions between the two geopolitical rivals are high over trade, artificial intelligence, Trump’s war with Iran and China’s designs on Taiwan.

articles.title_orig: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years for sexual assault after retrial
articles.title_zh: Harvey Weinstein sentenced to 15 years for sexual assault after retrial
articles.content_orig:
Harvey Weinstein has been sentenced to 15 years behind bars.
The disgraced movie mogul 's sentencing took place Wednesday, Sept. 23 in a New York federal court, one year after he was convicted of a first-degree criminal sexual act stemming from the assault of former production assistant Miriam Haley in 2006.
Haley shared her victim impact statement in court, saying Weinstein, 74, "abused his position and power," causing a "devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away," per multiple outlets, including NBC and CBS .
"Making the decision to speak up will have me looking over my shoulder for years to come," Haley added. "It's a life sentence for me."
Weinstein spoke as well, denying all allegations and apologizing to "anyone I may have hurt by my actions."
"I do have remorse for Miriam Haley's pain, but I have to reiterate my innocence," he said.
Weinstein was initially given a 23-year sentence for a 2020 conviction on rape and sexual assault charges, but the case was overturned four years later. The retrial took place in 2025, putting some of the defining accusations of his original #MeToo case back in the spotlight.
A 12-person jury ultimately handed down only one guilty verdict for Weinstein's crimes involving Haley, but did not deliver the same for the other two charges. He was acquitted of a second first-degree criminal sexual act stemming from his alleged assault of Kaja Sokola in 2002 when she was a 16-year-old aspiring actress.
The judge also declared a mistrial on a count of third-degree rape of Jessica Mann after one juror refused to continue deliberations, and prosecutors later declined to pursue another trial . In a June press release, Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg attributed the decision to focusing on getting justice through Weinstein's sentence in Haley's case.
"We also shared our recommendation to the court that Mr. Weinstein be sentenced to 20 years in prison, which would account for the significant harms his actions have caused Ms. Haley," Bragg said. "I want survivors of sexual violence in Manhattan to know that we believe you, and we will fight for you. We stand with survivors, today and every day."
Throughout his legal troubles, Weinstein has denied ever having nonconsensual sex or assaulting anyone. When the verdict for his retrial came in June 2025, his representative Juda Engelmayer said, "We take the wins where we get them. And the acquittal on the Sokola charge was a major one. A conviction there would have reset the sentencing clock entirely."
Engelmayer further noted the guilty first-degree criminal sexual act conviction should fall under time served, "and that clock is already running."
Weinstein, once a Hollywood institution, is currently serving a separate 16-year prison sentence after being found guilty of rape in a 2022 case in California.
If you or someone you know has experienced sexual violence, RAINN's National Sexual Assault Hotline offers free, confidential, 24/7 support in English and Spanish via chat and at 800-656-4673. If you or someone you know is a victim of domestic violence, call the National Domestic Violence Hotline at 800-799-7233 or text "START" to 88788.

articles.title_orig: U.N. Live Updates: Iran’s President Accuses U.S. and Israel of Lawless Attacks After Trump Threatens to 'Annihilate' Iran
articles.title_zh: U.N. Live Updates: Iran’s President Accuses U.S. and Israel of Lawless Attacks After Trump Threatens to 'Annihilate' Iran
articles.content_orig:
• Iran president speaks: In his UN General Assembly address, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said Iran will never bend to US President Donald Trump and asserted Iranians have been “the victims of terrorism.” A US delegate in the room walked out.
• Trump on Iran: The US president said yesterday that he faces a decision between annihilating Iran or making a deal to end the war. The US said delegations from both countries held talks on the sidelines through mediators.
• Zelensky gives remarks later: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said he was ready for trilateral talks with Russia and US to end the war in Ukraine, is also speaking today.
• Eyes on Venezuela: Venezuela’s acting President Delcy Rodríguez will address UNGA more than eight months after the US captured her predecessor, Nicolás Maduro, who is currently being held in a Brooklyn detention center. Trump met with her last night as Washington maintains political pressure on Venezuela to enact reforms.
Rubio says Putin invited to G20 summit in Miami
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Russian President Vladimir Putin has been invited to attend the G20 summit in Miami, Florida in December.
“We’ve invited President Putin to the G20. We think it’s an opportunity for him to engage not just with the president but with other world leaders. We hope that’s an invitation he’ll accept,” Rubio told reporters on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York.
If the Russian leader accepts the invitation it will be his first time attending the summit in-person since 2019, before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
“If there’s another opportunity for them to meet and there’s a purpose behind the meeting, that would be good,” Rubio said of a possible meeting between Putin and US President Donald Trump.
Why the Strait of Hormuz remains a critical sticking point in the Iran war
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian brought up the Strait of Hormuz earlier in his speech to the UN General Assembly. Months after the US and Israel launched the war with Iran, the strait remains at the center of the conflict and the global energy crisis.
Talks between Persian Gulf diplomats and Iranian officials — which were set to discuss an Omani plan for reopening the waterway to tanker traffic — were postponed indefinitely earlier this month.
Why it’s so significant: There are few places more strategically important to the global economy than the waterway, located between the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. Before the war, around 20% of global oil production flowed through the strait.
The waterway is only about 24 miles across at its narrowest point. Bolstered by sea mines, missiles and miles of coastline, Iran has long had the upper hand for controlling the shipping lane.
The US initially underestimated Iran’s willingness to close the strait — a strategic error that Tehran has capitalized on by leveraging its ability to threaten commercial shipping and prolong the war.
The current state-of-play: Despite shipping traffic remaining depressed, US President Donald Trump has insisted the state of the waterway is acceptable for now. In recent weeks, more tankers have moved through the strait due to the US military clearing mines and escorting vessels through the passage.
But commercial ships still face the threat of Iranian attacks, and there are questions around how long the US military can credibly maintain its substantial commitment of ships and resources to the strait.
What happens next: Trump administration officials have privately indicated they want to refocus negotiations on Tehran’s nuclear program and not reopening the strait, according to three sources familiar with the matter.
Iranian officials have signaled that they would be open to nuclear negotiations with the US — but only when the strait issue is resolved and the US lifts its blockade of Iranian ports, a regional source told CNN.
As a result, getting the ball rolling on a framework to reopen the waterway is likely a critical step to pave the way for talks on an overall end to the war.
CNN’s John Liu, Chris Isidore, Nadeen Ebrahim, Kylie Atwood, Zachary Cohen, Lauren Kent, Annette Choi and Jennifer Hansler contributed to this report.
Ahead of Zelensky's remarks at UNGA, catch up on the status of the war in Ukraine
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky will speak at the UN General Assembly later today.
Get up to speed on what’s been happening on the ground as Russia’s war in Ukraine grinds past four and a half years, with no sign of stopping anytime soon:
- No letup with strikes: Russia continues to hit Kyiv and other cities throughout Ukraine with drones and missiles, as Ukraine has been hammering Russian fuel infrastructure for months. Today, Russia targeted warehouses in Odesa, areas of Kyiv and a Zaporizhzhia shopping center. Over the weekend, Ukraine carried out its largest-ever drone attack on the Russian capital and surrounding area as voting in parliamentary elections entered the final day. Earlier this month, a Russian drone hit a train near Ukraine’s border with Poland as a group of former Western officials traveled out of the country, and NATO countries on the alliance’s eastern flank remain on high alert.
- Trump claims agreement: US President Donald Trump last Tuesday said Ukraine and Russia agreed to stop hitting each other’s energy targets amid concerns over the global spike in fuel prices — but both Zelensky and the Kremlin later described it as a proposal rather than a firm agreement.
- Russian missile attacks: Russia has increasingly been launching high-speed missile attacks across Ukraine, exploiting Kyiv’s shortage of US-made Patriot air defense interceptors. That shortage has been compounded by a global supply crunch due to the Iran war.
- Ukraine targets logistics hubs: Ukraine, meanwhile, has recently struck deep into Russian territory, sparking fuel shortages. Kyiv has also stepped up attacks on Ozon logistics hubs in Russia — a competitor to the frequently targeted e-commerce giant Wildberries — as it seeks to undermine Moscow’s war-driven economy.
- First visit from US envoys: Special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner pushed for a return to trilateral talks between the US, Russia and Ukraine in a meeting with top Ukrainian officials earlier this month, which marked their first trip to Kyiv since the war began. The talks followed intensive meetings between the US team and Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. Russia hit Kyiv a day after the visit.
CNN’s Laura Sharman, Svitlana Vlasova, Darya Tarasova, Ivana Kottasová, Sophie Tanno, Lex Harvey, Chris Isidore, Matt Egan, Nathan Hodge, Clare Sebastian, Zahra Ullah, Anna Chernova, Katharina Krebs, Kosta Gak, Sophie Tanno, Billy Stockwell and Victoria Butenko contributed reporting.
Rubio: 'No discussion' of extending US final withdrawal from Iraq
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there has been “no discussion” of extending the US’ final withdrawal from Iraq, which is slated for the end of this month.
The US military presence in Iraq is scheduled to officially end on September 30 after more than two decades, following a 2024 agreement to withdraw remaining troops after the end of the ISIS campaign.
Still, Baghdad has struggled to deal with the militias within its country. Iranian-backed militia in Iraq have launched waves of strikes on US and allied interests amid the war in Iran.
Rubio, who met with Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi at the UN General Assembly on Monday, said al-Zaidi did not ask the US to extend its presence.
President Donald Trump also saw al-Zaidi “briefly” on Tuesday night, Rubio told reporters in New York.
Responding to a question from CNN, Rubio said the US has “zero doubt” of al-Zaidi’s commitment to try to control the Iraqi militias but noted that it is “a massive challenge.”
The top US diplomat said the Iraqi prime minister has “achieved certain things” with regard to the militias,

articles.title_orig: Sources: Jaxson Dart to have season-ending knee surgery
articles.title_zh: Sources: Jaxson Dart to have season-ending knee surgery
articles.content_orig:
All offseason, New York Giants head coaches had hammered home the message to their quarterback: Protect yourself.
The Giants loved 2025 first-round pick Jaxson Dart's toughness, and they built an offense with plays designed to exploit the math problem his mobility creates for defenses.
No one told Dart not to run. But coaches and front-office members alike kept reminding Dart through spring and summer to slide at run's end. They reminded him to protect himself rather than lay his body on the line at comparatively inconsequential moments, as he had during his rookie year.
"You can't just say, 'Don't run the football here because you could get hurt' — you have to show him evidence," offensive coordinator Matt Nagy told Yahoo Sports in June. "Where did you take the extra hits? Was it necessary?
And then a cruel irony unfolded: In the second game of Dart's sophomore season, as he demonstrated the development of a passer cycling through his progressions, he suffered a season-ending injury anyway.
Sometimes, the violent game of football doesn't care.
Dart wasn't scrambling Monday night when, on the seventh snap of the game, he was crushed awkwardly. He wasn't even escaping the pocket to throw on the run.
Dart was dropping back, and winding up for a well-placed throw to tight end Theo Johnson on third-and-8, when edge rusher Byron Young swarmed from his left side and outside linebacker Josaiah Stewart closed in from Dart's right. As Young moved in for the tackle, Dart fell into Stewart.
Jaxson Dart is down on the field after this play. pic.twitter.com/R059M6kM6e
— TSN (@TSN_Sports) September 22, 2026
Dart lay on the ground, clutching his left knee, before eventually limping off without the help of staff or a cart. He even returned to the sideline in a gray hoodie and black turtleneck after initial tests indicated that no, his requests to return that night would not be granted, but there was at least optimism about the duration and severity of his injury.
A Tuesday MRI proved more daunting, the specter of season-ending surgery suddenly looming over the Giants and their quarterback. By Wednesday, per multiple reports, the decision was made: Dart will undergo surgery to repair damage to his meniscus, MCL and PCL. His ACL is intact.
Head coach John Harbaugh, whose appreciation for Dart strongly swayed his decision to join the Giants in January, is left to pick up the pieces of an offense now in the hands of Jameis Winston.
How much does a head coach's job change when his starting quarterback goes down?
"I think that's a pretty self-evident answer, isn't it?" Harbaugh told reporters Tuesday over Zoom, declining to confirm the severity or rehabilitation timeline of Dart's injury. "It's an important position, obviously. That's a pretty obvious answer.
"Just theoretically. I mean we're talking theory, I take it."
A key reason Harbaugh took Giants job: Jaxson Dart
After the Baltimore Ravens fired Harbaugh in January after 18 seasons, the landscape of a favorable market emerged. In a rare year, 10 NFL teams moved on from their coaches after the 2025 NFL season.
Harbaugh was the most attractive candidate by many metrics. He would have his choice among several suitors.
So Harbaugh wasn't going to team up with just any quarterback after enjoying success with two-time MVP Lamar Jackson. The Giants knew they needed to sell Harbaugh on their potential.
"We were trying to recruit him to come on a coaching visit," Giants general manager Joe Schoen told Yahoo Sports in June. "He had whoever his army of people were watching the offense, watching the defense, schematically. Also watching the individual talents. We didn't play Baltimore last year, so I'm not sure he realized how well Jaxson played throughout the season.
"I would say he was pleasantly surprised."
Harbaugh met with Dart in person for about 45 minutes during his interview process, Schoen said. The two watched film together, discussing both scheme and culture.
"I think I learned just how charismatic [Dart] is and how much he really wants to win," Harbaugh told Yahoo Sports of the meeting. "I also learned how dialed into what it takes [he is]. He was asking me some really, really good questions about how we're going to run things and I could just tell we're going to think alike. …
"He's all about doing what it takes."
Harbaugh now needs to do what his job takes without his most important player.
What are the Giants losing in Dart?
Dart finished his rookie year completing 63.7% of his passes for 2,272 yards, 15 touchdowns and 5 interceptions. He rushed for an additional 487 yards and nine scores, across his 14 total games that included 12 starts.
In a season-opening win against the Cowboys, Dart completed 79.3% of his pass attempts for 230 yards and three touchdowns while rushing 11 more times for 54 yards. The Giants did not turn over the ball in the 28-20 win.
Dart, whom coaches believed finished his rookie year with underrated anticipatory throwing, said he felt comfortable. Nagy praised his quarterback for his calm and composure making plays. Dart's 134.2 passer rating, albeit in one game, marked the most efficient game of his career by 24 points. Dart exploited Cowboys' weaknesses well, at one point targeting the left flat three times on the same series when he discerned the Giants' favorable leverage.
The Rams' defense would prove stiffer in a Week 2 "Monday Night Football" game, but Giants brass traveled to Los Angeles excited to see Dart rise to the occasion.
Instead, after five pass attempts in the first series, Dart was limping off. And while Winston was serviceable last season in two-and-a-half games of play, throwing for three touchdowns while scoring another two via rushing and receiving, he completed just 11 of 27 pass attempts (40.7%) for 111 yards, no scores and an interception in what became a 28-6 loss on Monday.
Harbaugh defended Winston, saying the team as a whole "didn't play up to that level across the board." A day after the loss, the coach continued to express faith in his quarterback.
"Absolute faith in all of our players," Harbaugh said. "That's why all the guys are here. Jameis is one of our guys who obviously is here for a reason. He's a very good football player."
Harbaugh: 'If you get punched in the gut, are you going down?'
There's reason to believe Winston's 2026 season could unfold better than his initial start.
While Winston's career has been characterized with entertaining highs and mind-boggling lows, there's reason to believe he can improve from his first outing.
To start: Any quarterback receiving first-team snaps throughout the week will be better prepared to navigate an opponent than a quarterback thrust into game action. Winston's difficulty transitioning could also reflect how different his play style is from that of Dart, for whom the Giants game plan vs. the Rams was designed. The Giants also struggled to run the ball against the Rams, mustering just 52 yards off 21 carries (2.5 yards per carry).
So while the Giants will look to tweak Winston's decision-making, precision and patience on certain plays, expect them also to prepare a game plan less reliant on a quarterback's dual-threat abilities than their plan last week. (In comparison, when Marcus Mariota replaced Washington Commanders quarterback Jayden Daniels against the Dallas Cowboys last weekend, Mariota's mobility translated better to zone-read principles on which Daniels thrives.)
Another reason for short-term encouragement about the Giants' chances to win without Dart: their schedule. Three of the Giants' next five opponents are currently 0-2, beginning with the Tennessee Titans who visit Sunday on the Giants' short week.
The other two are the Arizona Cardinals and New Orleans Saints, who have each split their first two contests.
The Giants have a chance to settle their offense and keep their season floor afloat.
Their ceiling, meanwhile, faces serious doubt.

articles.title_orig: Logitech’s new Blue Yeti 2 mic adjusts itself to where you are
articles.title_zh: Logitech’s new Blue Yeti 2 mic adjusts itself to where you are
articles.content_orig:
The original Blue Yeti has been one of the most recognizable go-to USB microphones for content creators since it launched in 2009, and now it finally has a successor. Launching today under Logitech G, the Blue Yeti 2 adds some modern upgrades, including an interactive LED display, AI de-noising, and a proximity based voice sensor — which resolves a notable flaw with its predecessor’s design while still paying homage to it.
Logitech’s new Blue Yeti 2 mic adjusts itself to where you are
The Blue Yeti’s successor is (hopefully) idiot-proofed for podcasters, YouTubers, and anyone else trying to be heard.
It’s available in black or white color options for $159.99, which is comparatively cheaper than Shure’s popular MV7 series USB microphones, which are the current choice for podcasters and start at $299. It’s also interestingly just $10 more than the original Blue Yeti’s launch price 17 years ago. A lot has happened since then, with Logitech acquiring the Blue audio production company for $117 million in 2018 and later killing the Blue brand entirely in 2023 when it merged the products with its own gaming-focused Logitech G sub brand. That means this new launch should just be called the Yeti 2, but Logitech clearly has some nostalgia to play with here.
The Blue Yeti 2 includes a built-in audio proximity sensor that tracks your voice in 3D, and automatically adjusts gain, EQ, and pickup patterns to preserve recording quality regardless of how close or far you are when moving around the mic. That should make this a more beginner friendly USB microphone than the original, as you don’t need to have any knowledge or experience with manually tweaking those settings to achieve optimal results. Plus, it still retains a similar design to the OG Yeti which confused people into incorrectly speaking into the top of it, an issue this new sensor should address.
It provides up to 24-bit / 48 kHz high-resolution capture. Other audio features include integrated direct digital signal processing (DSP) to improve voice clarity without additional software, and AI-powered noise removal to reduce unwanted background sounds like computer fans and mouse clicks. Given Logitech is pitching this to streamers, the 1.3-inch color LED display on the front where the controls are located also features a “Yeti character” that provides visual feedback on gain levels and polar patterns.

articles.title_orig: Logitech Just Unveiled Several New Gaming Accessories In Its Pro Line
articles.title_zh: Logitech Just Unveiled Several New Gaming Accessories In Its Pro Line
articles.content_orig:
Logitech just unveiled several new gaming accessories in its Pro line
There's a mouse, mousepad, keyboard and headset.
Logitech just introduced several new gaming accessories in its Pro line of products. This includes a mouse, keyboard, mousepad and headset.
First up, the Pro X3 Superstrike Mouse is a refresh of the highly-regarded Pro X2. This one prioritizes a longer battery life and offers a "significant leap in precision and elite control." Logitech promises a "lightweight, perfectly balanced chassis." The mouse uses the company's proprietary HITS technology, which is a haptic trigger system that replaces traditional microswitches. It'll be available on October 6 and costs $200.
There's also the Pro X Control Mousepad. The pad was made with specialized knitted cloth for "balanced, omnidirectional glide and precise control." It also includes a high-friction base for stability. The mousepad comes out on October 8 and costs $60.
The Pro X2 Rapid Gaming Keyboard features custom magnetic switches that allow for "granular tailoring of key sensitivity." It also boasts the company's Rapid Trigger technology, which resets a key the exact moment a finger begins to lift. This is great for competitive gaming, as it helps shave off a bit of time with every input.
The keyboard also integrates with Logitech's Key Priority system, which registers a secondary input without having to let go of the previous input. This is a boon for FPS players, as it makes it really easy to strafe and input directional changes. It's available right now for $230.
The Pro X3 Lightspeed Gaming Headset includes a "studio-grade 48kHz microphone" and a battery that lasts 70 hours per charge. That's a 40 percent increase when compared to the previous iteration. There's also now a 10-band EQ, accessible via proprietary G Hub software. It'll be available on October 8 for $250.

articles.title_zh: Logitech's Yeti 2 Brings The 17-Year-Old USB Mic Into The Modern Age
articles.content_orig:
Logitech's Yeti 2 brings the 17-year-old USB mic into the modern age
It adds a 3D proximity sensor, AI noise reduction and a 1.3-inch display.
Logitech is updating a classic. The Yeti 2 is a reimagined sequel to the original Blue Yeti USB microphone. Despite originally launching in 2009 (and spawning several offshoots), the OG Yeti is still a popular pick for podcasters, streamers and the like. The new model tries to modernize things with a 3D proximity sensor, AI-powered noise reduction and... an actual Yeti.
The Yeti 2's 3D proximity sensor is designed to make level and directional adjustments as brainless as possible. Logitech says it tracks your voice in space, automatically adjusting gain, EQ and pickup patterns as you move. Automatic gain and tracking are enabled out of the box.
Meanwhile, an onboard AI denoiser is designed to reduce unwanted background sounds like mouse clicks and keystrokes. If the whole package works as expected, this could make the mic friendlier for people who don't want to turn microphone levels into a hobby.
Speaking of friendly, meet your new pal, the Yeti, who lives on the mic's new 1.3-inch LED display. The mascot provides visual feedback on gain and directional patterns, aiming to make things more approachable. (I'm getting serious "Clippy for microphones" vibes.) As gimmicky as it may be, the mascot might make things easier to understand than a simple status light. If Yetis aren't your thing, custom avatars will be available through Logitech's G Hub software.
The mic has a redesigned three-capsule array, 24-bit / 48kHz recording, several directional modes and a headphone jack for monitoring. There's a capacitive mute button, a physical control dial and five stored presets.
The Logitech G Blue Yeti 2 is available now in black and white options. You can buy it for $160 from Logitech's website and third-party retail partners.

articles.title_orig: ‘I am the code’: Trump clashed with ballroom architect over safety issues
articles.title_zh: ‘I am the code’: Trump clashed with ballroom architect over safety issues
articles.content_orig:
When Donald Trump decided to pursue a giant White House ballroom, the president handpicked architect James McCrery, who runs a small firm known for its work designing Catholic cathedrals. It wasn’t long, however, before trouble emerged.
The more the Republican president started micromanaging the endeavor and expanding the scope of the vanity project, the more the shambolic process reportedly did not sit well with McCrery.
And so, late last year, Trump hired a new architect to oversee the initiative — one who presumably would be comfortable with the president’s appetite for the ever-expanding, wildly popular project.
We’re just now, however, getting a better sense of what transpired behind the scenes. The Washington Post reported:
In the weeks leading up to his resignation last year, the first architect on the White House ballroom clashed with President Donald Trump over design features that the architect believed violated building safety codes, according to two people with knowledge of the discussions and corroborating documents reviewed by The Washington Post.
James McCrery II withdrew from the project last October after warning repeatedly that Trump was insisting on a preliminary design that did not provide adequate emergency exit routes or fire-containment measures, said the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the private discussions.
According to the Post’s reporting, which has not been independently verified by MS NOW, the president heard the architect’s concerns but discounted them — not because he thought McCrery was wrong, but because he said building codes were irrelevant.
“I am the code,” Trump told him.
If accurate, the exchange was emblematic of a larger pattern in which the president has repeatedly made clear that he believes rules and limits apply to everyone except him.
“L’État, c’est moi” is a phrase attributed to France’s King Louis XIV, and 370 years later, the gap between “I am the state” and “I am the code” is narrow.

articles.title_orig: Xi Jinping appears to be leaving China's CEOs at home for his Washington trip
articles.title_zh: Xi Jinping appears to be leaving China's CEOs at home for his Washington trip
articles.content_orig:
As recently as last week, Chinese President Xi Jinping was expected to arrive in Washington with a large delegation of Chinese CEOs, as President Trump touted a dealmaking atmosphere surrounding the two leaders' summit.
Now, Xi is scheduled to arrive this evening with a significantly smaller business delegation in tow, dampening expectations even as an array of US executives remains set to be on hand for the gathering.
Chinese state media announced Xi's departure for the US on Wednesday, noting only a small entourage that included family members and political aides.
The South China Morning Post reported that a lack of progress on deals had led to the paring back of the list from the Chinese side.
US industry leaders had been expecting a wide array of Chinese business leaders to be in attendance from electric car makers and agriculture companies.
A White House official didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. Trump's team previously confirmed Thursday's state dinner would include Sam Altman of OpenAI (OPAI.PVT), Jensen Huang of Nvidia (NVDA), and Elon Musk of Tesla (TSLA).
The summit is set to begin this evening, when Trump will travel to Joint Base Andrews to greet Xi when he arrives at 6 p.m. ET.
The tone shift around business deals comes as other policy areas like AI and trade are expected to see only small steps forward, and signs emerge that Trump is set to roll out the red carpet for the Chinese leader.
Close observers of US-China relations have noted that Xi did not do the same when Trump visited Beijing in May, sending a subordinate for Trump's arrival.
Some of the US CEOs set to attend this week's festivities, including Huang and Musk, traveled with Trump to Beijing earlier this year.
Members of both leaders' economic teams are set to be in attendance, including US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, who met in New York over the weekend.
Bessent left that meeting describing the talks as constructive and saying the US had proposed a new AI safety "notification mechanism" that could allow Bessent and He and other officials to communicate quickly in the event of an incident related to AI. But China has yet to publicly embrace the idea.
The lack of further progress on AI underscored the modest ambitions of this week's summit that might be high on pomp and circumstance but light on policy.
There is little expectation of the US or China agreeing to broader limits on AI, such as regulating frontier models. In fact, both sides have signaled that they are eager to race forward with the technology.
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Bucks reportedly being investigated by NBA for possible salary-cap circumvention in deal with Gary Trent Jr.
articles.title_zh: Bucks reportedly being investigated by NBA for possible salary-cap circumvention in deal with Gary Trent Jr.
articles.content_orig:
When the Milwaukee Bucks agreed to sign Gary Trent Jr. to a four-year, $64 million deal in July, red flags went up all around the league's office. Days later, reports emerged suggesting the NBA was looking into the signing, though details of the league's probe were scarce.
The league apparently found enough that it decided to launch a full-on investigation, according to The Athletic. The focus of that investigation: whether the Bucks used the contract as a way to circumvent the NBA salary cap.
The league reportedly hired law firm Hecker Fink to perform that investigation.
That particular accusation should sound familiar, as the league just wrapped an investigation on the Los Angeles Clippers and Kawhi Leonard that looked into the exact same thing. While both teams were accused of the same violation, their methods for allegedly circumventing the salary cap differ.
In the Clippers' case, the team was accused of using a team sponsor to funnel additional funds to Leonard as a way to get around NBA rules. Accusations surrounding the Bucks are far more straight forward.
The league is reportedly looking into whether the Bucks made handshake agreements with Trent to sign lesser deals the past two offseasons with the promise of Trent eventually receiving a much larger contract this offseason.
The issue stems from Trent's massive pay increase this offseason. After making $2.6 million with the Bucks in 2024 and $3.7 million in 2025, Trent's new deal will pay him an average of over $15 million the next four years.
That massive pay increase came after Trent experienced a down season, one in which he averaged just 8.1 points per game, his lowest scoring output since his rookie season.
When reached for comment by The Athletic, the NBA, Bucks and Trent's agency — Klutch Sports — all declined comment. Both the Bucks and Klutch are reportedly working with the NBA as it performs its investigation, per The Athletic.
Should the NBA determine the Bucks purposefully engaged in salary-cap circumvention, the team could see a similar punishment to the Clippers. The NBA came down hard on Los Angeles, docking the team five future first-round picks, fining and suspending team owner Steve Ballmer and fining Leonard.

Xbox appears to be ready to launch its own version of PlayStation’s platinum trophies. A new update to the Xbox PC app has revealed Mythic Achievements, which according to data in the app will appear once a player completes all the Achievements in a game.

Xbox CEO Asha Sharma revealed last month that Xbox would be getting a platinum trophy equivalent later this year. Microsoft still hasn’t officially announced Mythic Achievements, but if they’re already starting to appear in early Xbox software then you can bet they’ll turn up officially very soon.
Mythic Achievements started appearing in the Xbox PC app on the same day Microsoft announced it was laying off 268 Xbox staffers , likely closing Ninja Theory, and moving Halo , Sea of Thieves , and Age of Empires over to Activision .

articles.title_orig: McDonald’s Pledges Multibillion-Dollar Investment to Help Franchisees
articles.title_zh: McDonald’s Pledges Multibillion-Dollar Investment to Help Franchisees
articles.content_orig:
McDonald's (MCD) has one final shot this year to supersize its stock price.
And that Hail Mary toss will happen in Chicago on Wednesday at a closely watched investor day.
"We think the Sep 23 Investor Day could prove a crucial clearing event in which management articulates a credible path to reaccelerating same-store sales in the 4Q/2027, protecting & growing operating margins (w/ potential SG&A leverage starting next year), and still accelerating unit growth despite the tough macro," Jefferies analyst Andy Barish wrote. "For the stock to rebound, management will have to convince investors the recent same-store sales slowdown is fixable (soon) and restore confidence in the long-term growth algo."
It has been a dreadful year for the Golden Arches — one punctuated by an 18% drop in the stock price.
Comparable sales for a resurgent Restaurant Brands International-owned (QSR) Burger King US rose 8.5% year over year, beating analyst expectations, per Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace data. The result trounced McDonald's US result, which reported a disappointing 0.8% comparable sales gain.
McDonald's entered the fall with a black eye, given the barrage of key initiatives it recently launched and plans to launch.
First, McDonald's debuted its new McValue menu by offering 10 items under $3.
It then launched six new drinks on May 6, with refreshers like Strawberry Watermelon and crafted sodas like Sprite Berry Blast. All the drinks are caffeinated and aimed at Gen Z consumers who have been going to the nearest Dutch Bros (BROS) or convenience store for a Celsius (CELH).
A nationwide Aug. 17 rollout of its Red Bull Dragonberry Energizer ensued.
But the revamped McValue platform, discounted breakfast offers, and broader push into specialty beverages all failed to generate the incremental traffic McDonald's was banking on in the second quarter.
Investors are hoping to hear a different tune tomorrow.
"While lower-income consumer trends and highly promotional QSR environment don't provide much support, we view strategic missteps as largely responsible for the recent slowdown in same-store sales/traffic, much or all of which can be addressed in the 4Q and '27 to reaccelerate trends," Barish wrote.
"We expect a relatively quick adjustment to the marketing and menu innovation calendars that drove execution issues in the summer as management and franchisees return to a workable balance (some digital promos returned Aug 10, Spicy Chicken McNuggets limited-time offer came back Sept. 1, Spongebob x One Piece promo starts 9/15)," Barish added. "Work around franchisee pricing and participation in promos and value offerings could take longer, we expect an update on convos w/ franchisees next week. Finally, growing awareness of the new premium bevs (Red Bull launched Aug 17), Rewards, digital/delivery, and EDAP provides at least a steady floor."

articles.title_orig: Harvey Weinstein is set to be sentenced for sexual assault after 6-year legal odyssey
articles.title_zh: Harvey Weinstein is set to be sentenced for sexual assault after 6-year legal odyssey
articles.content_orig:
Estimated read time: 5-6 minutes
- Harvey Weinstein received a 15-year prison sentence for a 2006 sex crime.
- Weinstein, 74, was convicted of assaulting Miriam Haley, a former TV assistant.
- Judge Curtis Farber labeled Weinstein "a sexual predator" and "face of MeToo."
NEW YORK — Harvey Weinstein, the disgraced movie mogul, was sentenced in Manhattan to 15 years in prison Wednesday for a felony sex crime in another #MeToo reckoning.
Weinstein's sentencing for sexually assaulting one-time TV production assistant Miriam Haley followed a legal odyssey spanning more than six years. His 2020 conviction was overturned by New York's highest court. A second jury found Weinstein guilty again at a retrial last year.
Once among the most powerful figures in the entertainment industry, Weinstein was an Oscar-winning producer whose hits included "Shakespeare in Love," "Pulp Fiction" and "Chocolat." But his downfall came quickly after sexual assault allegations in 2017 set off the #MeToo movement.
Weinstein, 74, is expected to appeal and maintains that he never raped or sexually assaulted anyone. He is now likely to remain behind bars well into his 80s. Seated in a wheelchair, he was quickly moved out of the courtroom after the sentencing, while some of his accusers hugged and brushed away tears.
Weinstein and his victim both spoke in court
Weinstein faced up to 25 years in prison for sexually assaulting Haley at his Manhattan apartment in 2006. He has already served more than six years as his case cycled through the criminal justice system. Haley gave her account of the assault at two trials, and again addressed the court Wednesday.
"Having been sexually assaulted by Harvey Weinstein has had a devastating effect on my life and sense of security that may never go away. Making the decision to speak up will have me looking over my shoulder for years to come," Haley said.
"It's a life sentence for me," she added.
Minutes later, Weinstein apologized while reiterating his innocence.
"Reflecting on all that has happened since 2017 has helped me recognize how my past conduct has negatively affected others. I live with many regrets and sincerely apologize to anyone I have affected with my actions," he said.
Some of his accusers who were in court shook their heads while he spoke.
Weinstein is the face of MeToo, judge says
Judge Curtis Farber said Weinstein was once a king in the movie industry, "but recognition for these achievements will pale in comparison to what you did."
He said Weinstein is now known as "a sexual predator, the literal face of the MeToo movement."
The judge said Weinstein treated women as "mere objects to be played with and discarded" and still hasn't accepted responsibility, portraying himself as a victim during jailhouse interviews.
Haley afterward said she was happy with the sentence, while saying it's clear that Weinstein has not acknowledged what he did. "I think he still feels entitled, and that's part of the problem," she said.
Haley's lawyer, the famed victims' rights attorney Gloria Allred, rejected any suggestion that Weinstein's sentencing means the MeToo era is over.
"Women are empowered in a way they have never been before," she said.
Why Weinstein is being sentenced a second time
Weinstein was originally sentenced to 23 years in prison after a jury convicted him of assaulting Haley and raping an aspiring actress, Jessica Mann, in 2013.
Tried for a second time last year, he was again convicted of a first-degree criminal sex act for assaulting Haley, who has also gone by the name Mimi Haleyi. In a messy split verdict, the jury acquitted him of forcibly performing oral sex on another woman, Kaja Sokola, and could not reach a verdict on a rape charge involving Mann.
After another retrial ended in a hung jury in May, Manhattan prosecutors dropped the rape charge rather than pursue a fourth trial after Mann said she could not bear to testify again.
Weinstein's health issues pushed the defense to ask for leniency
Defense lawyer Jacob Kaplan wanted three more years on top of the six years Weinstein already served, saying a longer sentence would make it more likely that Weinstein dies in prison.
Weinstein has been in the hospital six times since 2025, Kaplan said, while dealing with blood cancer, congestive heart failure, and kidney issues.
Weinstein is also awaiting resentencing in a separate rape case in Los Angeles. A California appeals court upheld the 2022 conviction but threw out his original 16-year sentence because the judge had considered his New York convictions — that were later thrown out — as an aggravating factor.
After shuffling between state prison, where he tested positive for COVID-19 early in the pandemic, and New York City's notorious Rikers Island complex, Weinstein has been housed at a medical unit for inmates at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan.
Haley describes the assault that led to Weinstein's conviction
Haley, 49, is a former entertainment producer now working in advertising.
She said she met Weinstein through a mutual connection and worked briefly as a production assistant on "Project Runway," a reality competition show that he produced.
Haley said she accepted an invitation to visit Weinstein's apartment and after chatting briefly, he lunged to kiss her, she testified. She said she rebuffed him, but he grabbed her, forcibly backed her into a bedroom and sexually assaulted her, ignoring her pleas to stop.
She recalled Weinstein asking, "Don't you think we're much closer now?" after either the alleged assault or a subsequent occasion when she says she had unwanted, but not forced, sex with him.
She also recalled telling him after the second encounter, "You know you can't keep doing this."
The Associated Press does not typically identify people who say they are victims of sexual assault unless they grant permission, which Haley, Sokola and Mann have done.

articles.title_orig: China ‘throwing gasoline on the fire’ in AI data centers race, say lawmakers
articles.title_zh: China ‘throwing gasoline on the fire’ in AI data centers race, say lawmakers
articles.content_orig:
FIRST ON FOX: As President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping about the future of artificial intelligence, two top House Republicans are warning that the Chinese Communist Party is "throwing gasoline on the fire" by undermining America's effort to build out AI infrastructure.
In a new letter disclosed to Fox News Digital, House Ways and Means Committee Chairman Jason Smith, R-Mo., and House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party Chairman John Moolenaar, R-Mich., asked Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and IRS Chief Executive Officer Frank Bisignano to determine whether money has been funneled from overseas through America’s charitable system to block the data centers needed for the U.S. to compete with China.
Specifically, they raised questions about hundreds of millions of dollars that American-born communist tech tycoon Neville Roy Singham pumped into nonprofits and organizations that are now among the leading organizations fighting data center development throughout the country. Recipients of Singham's largesse include the Party for Socialism and Liberation and the ANSWER Coalition, both self-described pro-China communist groups. Earlier this month, activists from both groups carried signs in a Chapel Hill, N.C., protest, merging anti-Trump sentiments with support for communist Cuba and opposition to data centers and AI development, including the message, "SHUT IT DOWN!"
"Under no circumstances can we allow an adversary, and our most serious competitor in AI infrastructure, to weaponize our own tax code and harm an emerging American industry," the lawmakers wrote in the letter, sent on Tuesday.
FROM AUSTIN TO NEW YORK, PRO-CHINA NETWORK FUELS WEEK OF ANTI-US PROTESTS AS XI MEETS TRUMP
The lawmakers allege that influence operations linked to China are exploiting tax-exempt organizations, nonprofit networks and social media campaigns to fuel opposition to the data centers needed to power America’s AI industry.
The lawmakers urged the agencies to investigate whether tax-exempt organizations connected to the network have operated for the "private or political benefit of foreign-aligned interests" and whether donor-advised funds and intermediary entities were used to "launder the origin of foreign-directed money into American advocacy."
A Fox News Digital investigation found that Singham funneled $285 million since 2017 to six U.S. nonprofits, including his wife Jodie Evans' group, CodePink, through two shell corporations and a donor-advised philanthropy fund run by Goldman Sachs, which said it closed the Singham account in 2024.
The nonprofits have functioned with tax-deductible status while actively involved in promoting communist regimes such as China, coordinating street protests and fomenting anti-American rage. They have denied being part of any foreign influence operation, and Singham hasn't responded to requests for comment.
Smith said China is helping fuel opposition to American artificial intelligence infrastructure by giving a base to Singham as he funds U.S. nonprofit groups involved in anti-data-center protests.
"This is the Chinese helping throw the gasoline on the fire," Smith told Fox News Digital. "The American people need to know that this is not just an organic movement."
Smith said Americans have legitimate concerns about data centers, including their effect on electricity costs and water usage. But he said foreign-backed organizations shouldn't be allowed to exploit those concerns to slow U.S. technological development.
Smith said that "the Chinese want to stall and slow down the advancement of AI in the United States because they want to win the AI war."
"Tax exempt is a privilege. It is not a right," Smith said. "We need to make sure that we’re not subsidizing tax dollars to help create hostility and unrest in our country."
Smith also called for greater transparency regarding the flow of money among organizations connected to Singham. He added that the broader issue extends beyond the tax code and could include questions about compliance with the Foreign Agents Registration Act violations. "Transparency is the biggest thing," he said.
PROBE INTO 'SUBVERSIVE' ANTI-AI SINGHAM NETWORK IS 'ENORMOUS,' FORMER TREASURY ADVISOR SAYS
Moolenaar said organizations presenting themselves as grassroots opposition groups are actually advancing the Chinese Communist Party’s agenda in the U.S. "Groups that portray themselves as grassroots are really more AstroTurf — very fake — being funded by entities that are working in partnership with the Chinese Communist Party," Moolenaar told Fox News Digital.
"The concern is that they are manipulating the messaging and opposition to different American investments, whether it’s data centers or other technological advances, trying to turn the American people against these technologies so that China would be able to have dominance in this area," he said.
Moolenaar pointed to the use of grassroots organizations, community groups, propaganda and online bots.
"We don’t want foreign entities of concern — countries that may be opposed to American interests — using our system against the American people and trying to manipulate them," Moolenaar said.
He said the lawmakers are seeking greater transparency into the organizations’ funding and tax-exempt status, including whether their political activity violates federal rules.
"When you see them actively speaking out against American interests and realize that groups like CodePink are aggressively funded by this network, that raises serious concerns," Moolenaar said.
The chairman said China’s influence efforts exploit the openness of American society.
"The Chinese Communist Party always has the goal of dividing Americans, manipulating and getting their propaganda out," he said. "They don’t have the freedoms that we enjoy, and they try to exploit our freedoms and use that against us."
China remains both a major trading partner and a strategic competitor, Moolenaar said, but the United States must avoid becoming dependent on Beijing.
"They are a serious adversary," he said. "They are a trading partner, which is true, and we need to have a relationship with them," Moolenaar said. "But at the same time, we do not want to be manipulated, we do not want to become more dependent, and we certainly do not want to be under their thumb."
The lawmakers noted that a bicameral group of congressional committees, including the Ways and Means Committee, the House Select Committee on the CCP and the Senate Intelligence Committee, has been examining how influence operations linked to the CCP allegedly exploit America’s tax-exempt sector to "sow discord and undermine our democracy."
"The CCP consistently identifies political issues under public debate in our country and seeks to corrupt those debates," Smith and Moolenaar wrote in their letter. The CCP, they added, seeks to "heighten divisions between Americans and to degrade our civic processes."
The lawmakers specifically pointed to opposition campaigns targeting the construction of data centers, which are critical to the nation’s AI infrastructure.
A June report from OpenAI identified two clusters of ChatGPT accounts likely originating in China that were used in covert influence operations targeting U.S. debates over AI and technology policy. One campaign, dubbed "Data Center Bandwagon," generated social media comments and images claiming that data-center construction was raising electricity prices for average families. OpenAI said it found no evidence that the operation achieved meaningful breakout beyond its own activity, but said it demonstrated how foreign operators can exploit existing local concerns to amplify distrust.
